Furthermore, the text provides specific, detailed calculations regarding the creation and initial assessment of this random vortex system, specifically in the context of a flow within a two-dimensional channel and at infinite temporal duration.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with M modes, facilitating a description of its initial state using generalized coherent states. Due to its polynomial scaling with M, it is now possible to study Renyi entanglement entropies for systems containing large numbers of modes and moderate numbers of particles. Our findings include the existence of Renyi index-independent, symmetric Page curves, where maximum entropy occurs when the partition is even, as well as the linear increase in minimum entropy at fixed Renyi index, occurring when the partition is odd.

Temporal sequence analysis via supervised learning is gaining momentum in life science research. A new supervised learning framework converts the prediction task into a learning problem for high-dimensional temporal sequences. The framework trains a model that maximizes the prediction of future sequence values given past sequence values. The framework's effectiveness is tested using simulated and real-world datasets from proteomics, where the objective is to predict the future peptide detection statuses from past detection statuses during a mass spectrometry experiment. Compared to the existing method on a proteomics dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates improved accuracy on various simulated datasets and a prominent protein expression-related breast cancer dataset. The framework's source code is available for public use.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, empirical evidence indicates that human experts often rely on simplified representations when confronting complex systems, instead of trying to model them exactly. A potential technique for uncovering these representations is transfer learning, where an agent uses experience from one environment to succeed in another. This article presents a novel algorithm, the Recursive Partially Observable Markov Process, designed to learn these simplified representations and facilitate this transfer of knowledge. It works by identifying the underlying probabilistic processes from partial observations and using hidden states to improve its understanding of these processes. This RP2 algorithm can then use this understanding to make its actions more effective, even in complex systems that it has not encountered before. It uses a valuation function to determine near-optimal actions, but in contrast to previous methods, it does so based on a simplified representation of the underlying system, rather than attempting to accurately model the system's rules. The authors demonstrate that this algorithm is capable of uncovering these simplified representations and achieving near-optimal results, as illustrated in experiments involving partial observations and hidden states. It also has applications in other areas, such as uncovering the simplifying representations used by human experts and facilitating the transfer of knowledge between environments.

In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D CNNs.  However, this approach underestimates the significance of contextual information, assuming that a video's neighborhood has no influence on its classification.  This paper argues the opposite, claiming that contextual information is vital for accurate action detection.  To incorporate context effectively, we develop a model integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks and apply it to a weakly-supervised action detection framework.  By incorporating self-attention, the model increases the weight of important spatial features while reducing the impact of unimportant ones, thereby enhancing feature extraction.  Experimental evaluations of Kinetics and Kinetics-50 action datasets demonstrate the model's superiority in action detection tasks.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, it represented one of the largest and most complex image copy detection competitions ever held, incorporating two separate tracks for open-source and commercial submissions. Following this competition, a comprehensive review of the findings revealed the strengths and limitations of the participating approaches, paving the way for future developments in the field of image copy detection. This paper provides an overview of the challenge's framework, reports the winning results, and examines the various algorithmic strategies employed, aiming to guide the development of more advanced techniques for detecting copied content.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, and a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Understanding the behavior of such stochastic processes plays a significant role in the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations that incorporate a small parameter. In this context, metastability effects emerge when the size of the perturbation becomes significantly small. Our work encompasses a range of mathematical operators that incorporate singular degeneration at the boundary, encompassing normal, tangential, and interstitial types. These mathematical operators enable the analysis of stochastic processes that reflect anisotropic medium properties, specifically in situations where a non-degenerate perturbation is present. These phenomena have practical implications in various areas, including physical and biological sciences.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle of approximately $-58.2$ MeV at a mean field of $0.904$ fm. As the magnetic field increases, we observed a decrease in the mean field from $0.904$ fm and its radius tends to vanish at higher field intensities. Moreover, we found that the absence of a magnetic field results in a mean field-pressure relationship characterized by a soft nature. As the magnetic field intensity increases, the energy per particle exhibits an anisotropic distribution and its density features an egg-like shape, indicating highly denser regions at the poles.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework for neural networks. Unlike traditional compression methods that distort data, REC compresses data without alteration before transmission and recovers it accurately at the receiver's end. We proved the effectiveness of REC in achieving both efficient communication and data protection by providing the first known differential privacy guarantee for any compression method. Based on this proof, we designed DP-REC, a novel framework for distributed neural network training that provides a reliable differential privacy guarantee while minimizing communication costs. In our experimental evaluation, we showed that DP-REC provides the first known differential privacy guarantee for any compression method while achieving significant reductions in communication overhead, comparable to the state-of-the-art performance achieved by the recent Compression-Attack Mitigation (CAM) method.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at nearly identical wavelengths. The UV intensity of the region was measured and compared to H$\alpha$ emission to identify dense molecular cloud boundaries and background radiation patterns. Elevated UV levels were discovered near Taurus-Auriga and Perseus, reaching approximately 15 times the expected interstellar value. This was attributed to the presence of additional stars within these regions. A model estimating the UV radiation intensity based on star count and distance also failed to capture the observed magnitude of the UV flux, indicating the presence of additional UV sources or dust emission in these areas. A FIMS image of the region also revealed a bright UV spot, SH2-261, which was found not to be associated with an ISM filament but rather caused by stellar radiation from $\tau$ Per. Another area of interest, located near CO emission, was found to display a gradient that could be the result of foreground interstellar radiation or an undetected UV source.

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy.

This paper delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), which expands on the single-period model developed by Fudenberg and Stacchetti (1996). Their theory reveals that in multi-stage games of incomplete information, players' expectations of others' expectations can form an infinite chain, known as a 'cognitive hierarchy'. The study shows that a simple model incorporating this hierarchy accurately predicts the Nash equilibrium in various three-person games involving action and contribution decisions. Findings indicate that players' expectations of others' expectations converge to zero. The research also discovers that stronger prior assumptions lead to faster convergence of the cognitive hierarchy and more precise predictions of Nash behavior. Additionally, the study validates the robustness of the dynamic cognitive hierarchy model by experimenting with different parameters and uncovering instances where players' expectations and expectations of others' expectations diverge.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically in two districts of Mozambique ($\sim$1,800 km$^2$), using population counts from the 2020 census and previous estimates from the National Statistics Institute as references. We evaluated six estimation methods and found three validated approaches which we will make available as an open-source tool. We found that population density was the determining factor in our population counting model and found models built with suspiciously accurate population microcensus data proved more effective than those using census data. We found the best tool to be SimpleImplemantation of a convolutional neural network (CNN), providing a reliable solution despite the challenges of the suspension of censuses and ongoing pandemic.

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the avoidance of potential errors in data queries for specific elements. This research aims to introduce a new type of static filter that eliminates incorrect positive results for negative data sets, showcasing how it can be efficiently implemented with xor and static hash tables. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of adaptive solutions in reducing errors over existing technologies, while compared to state-of-the-art solutions that guarantee no errors, our proposed approach achieves comparable storage efficiency.

We have theoretically analyzed an original process in which a fragment of two atoms in a state of entanglement with a hyperfine degree of freedom can combine with another atom to create a molecule also in a state of entanglement with the same degree of freedom. This process in our model relies on the manipulation of three energy levels. We have successfully applied the multi-structure model and discovered three-body recombination probabilities that exhibit properties of entanglement mixing, as well as distinct characteristics based on symmetry, and we found that the molecule formed can exist in states of relative angular momentum of -1, 0, or 1. Moreover, the conditions necessary for creating molecules in states of relative angular momenta of +1 and 0 are significantly reduced in comparison to those required for creating them in a state of relative angular momentum of -1. Our model can be used to create atoms in states of relative angular momentum of -1 through the interaction of atoms in states of relative angular momentum of 0 and -2. This process can be realized through the manipulation of tri-atomic gases with the application of optical pulses with a power of hundreds of thousands of watts and a duration of several microseconds, or by manipulating a gas of tri-atomic molecules with the application of pulses with the intensity of a Wannier state with a duration of a millisecond.

Spherical harmonic-based SPH approach, known for its accurate representation of conserved quantities, has been enhanced with multiple resolution capabilities facilitated by the use of spherical harmonic bases of varying degrees. In typical SPH simulations, the order of these degrees can be set uniformly for the entire domain, yet this study introduces a way to dynamically change the order within and across sub-domains. By doing so, a higher order scheme can effectively identify where high resolution is needed while a lower order scheme can increase efficiency when coarser grids are used in other areas. Moreover, this framework allows for the identification of where to impose specific numerical constraints. By preserving key fluid dynamics principles, the framework's implementation doesn't alter the underlying SPH discretization. Its feasibility has been confirmed through both theoretical and practical evidence. A crucial aspect of this framework involves efficiently communicating between sub-domains, and implementing a significant data reduction mechanism simplifies this process. Additionally, mathematical optimizations have been applied to mitigate potential performance issues. Furthermore, when testing the framework against analytical data, the results showed excellent agreement. By integrating this framework with existing SPH frameworks, it can significantly enhance simulation efficiency while maintaining accuracy. Moreover, when paired with existing FSI methodologies, it enables novel approaches to simulating FSI interactions, particularly with complex geometries and non-conforming interfaces, and allows for the efficient modeling of fluid and structure interaction at both the component and system levels.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. Advances in quantum computing may offer a solution to this problem, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to achieve computational advantages. Researchers have initially focused on applying quantum computing to classification tasks, whereas learning important aspects of data, i.e., correlations and probabilistic relationships, remains largely unexploited. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of variational circuits on superconducting quantum processors for both unsupervised and supervised clustering tasks on random datasets. Moreover, researchers have successfully applied these methods to real-world data, including a dataset on types of glass, showcasing a competitive error rate compared to traditional machine learning approaches.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught to recognize speech with a range of pitches all for the same sentence.  Experimental results show that these algorithms help make FastPitch easier to control.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they are obscured, covered or carried by other objects. Currently prevalent deep learning based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when applied to video-based reasoning problems. We introduce a model named Hopper that employs a multi-hop transformer to deduce object persistence in videos by iteratively skipping key frames to accurately predict the final location of the target object, given both video content and localization information. Furthermore, our proposed model benefits from using a contrastive loss for robust, high-level frame representations. Hopper's simplicity and effectiveness allow it to tackle various video-based reasoning challenges with exceptional precision and efficiency, outperforming other prominent methods across both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The investigation encompasses various factors, including a detailed understanding of the underlying physics that isn't typically accounted for in predictions (other processes beyond direct production), a more accurate calculation of the process (not limited to tree-level terms). The research utilizes a specific simulation model for these factors and a more precise calculation of the process (based on matrix elements up to the next level). The investigation involves comparing predicted outcomes from the three main theories for the same process (not necessarily identical in the context of the underlying physics and other factors) to data from the LHC, with a focus on determining the mass of the W boson. Specifically, it compares predicted outcomes based on different assumptions for the mass of the W boson (16,520; 16,580; 16,580; 16,590; 16,592; 16,593; 16,593; 16,594; 16,596; 16,597; 16,598; 16,600; 16,605; 16,608; 16,615; 16,622; 16,625; 16,628; 16,632; 16,635; 16,640; 16,644; 16,648; 16,652; 16,655; 16,658

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A crucial factor for these robots' acceptance is ensuring users have a satisfying experience while interacting remotely, including effortless navigation. This research focuses on an overlooked aspect of remote control: the navigation aspect. An extensive study evaluated the Quality of Experience (QoE) for using Telepresence robots via the internet by combining it with a widely used audio quality metric, MOS-ULA. The results revealed that users' perceptions of the navigation process can be quite sensitive, with scores ranging from poor to excellent. Additionally, we discovered that dropping internet packets can negatively affect the navigation experience in terms of user satisfaction. This comprehensive understanding of the navigation QoE will help designers create satisfying interactive experiences for users operating these robots.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly explaining their Bayesian foundations and mathematically defining each stage within the hierarchy. We start with a Bayesian linear regression model, expanding it to a Bayesian hierarchical linear regression model and then integrating a prior into the analysis. Our focus lies in a single-level hierarchical regression model linking two groups of observations. Furthermore, we examine another model incorporating both fixed and random effects. Through a simulated dataset, we demonstrate the efficacy of the Bayesian hierarchical regression models at distinguishing fixed and random effects.

The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken, with lynching occurring during the day phase. Mafia members possess special abilities only active at night. This paper focuses on a standard version of the game with a specific number of participants, namely two mafia members and an indefinite count of citizens. Both players and mafia members possess identical decision-making tools, namely, they both use the same rules of probability. This work seeks to address the following queries: 1) Can the mafia be pinpointed? 2) Will the mafia be killed? This is a work involving basic elements of mathematical induction, probability, and reliability theory, aiming to provide a comprehensive overview of the game's fundamental principles.

Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the
formation of gaps in the disk. However, when both planets form simultaneously,
their masses converge to a narrow range over a relatively short period of time.
Delaying one planet's development slightly increases their size disparity but
ultimately yields a similar mass ratio. To replicate observed exoplanet mass
variations, models suggest planets form and grow at different times and then
exit the gas-accretion phase at varying points. If one planet develops ahead of
the other and then pauses, and the second planet continues to grow, this could
result in a large mass disparity. Furthermore, simulations indicate that gas-accretion
pause due to disk clearance may lead to the formation of unique, dense regions
in the disk surrounding giant planets, and these areas could potentially impact
the development of nearby small rocky planets, making areas with dense gas more
attractive to these planets.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent
nanoscale objects. Heat units known as phonons exhibit a dual influence on
conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating electron propagation through a complex energy terrain. 
In rare, high-quality carbon nanotubes with uniform properties, we have
distinguished between the typical scattering effect and a boosted transport mode, 
wherein electron excitation or de-excitation accompanies electron transfer without 
increasing the overall electric current. This boosted transport mode arises due to 
interactions between electrons in adjacent tubes, an effect predicted to be more 
prominent in films consisting of seeds of single-walled carbon nanotubes. 
Our observations support the existence of these boosted transport mechanisms 
in single-wall carbon nanotubes at various temperatures and also demonstrate 
their similarity to dual-channel conductivity behavior predicted for nanotube 
assemblies. Yet, further research is needed to assess the precise contribution 
of these boosted transport mechanisms to overall conductivity and to explore its 
potential in diverse materials.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple separate sub-spaces. Each sub-space consists of specific key characteristics that form variable, interconnected features. To effectively cluster such data, we create a fuzzy clustering algorithm that calculates a weighted similarity measure based on entropy, considers the reliability of each feature, and applies Lagrange multipliers to derive the optimal cluster boundaries. We evaluate the proposed method's performance in a 10% erroneous noise environment and compare it to six state-of-the-art algorithms using ten different datasets from various domains. Experimental findings demonstrate the superiority of this approach, achieving significantly better accuracy and larger benchmark performance gaps compared to traditional methods, with a notable 2.1% to 45.5% performance improvement over the entropy-based algorithm alone.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. However, traditional learning methods that utilize maximum likelihood have resulted in a fundamental statistical impairment - models that can accurately recognize separated data sets cannot reliably distinguish between identical, uniformly-distributed random noise and data. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed and tested two new algorithms. When tested on real-world datasets, the new methods significantly outperformed existing approaches. Not only do these methods yield better results, but they are also grounded in a unique form of model simplification, enabling us to understand the underlying statistical limitations of MoE models for the first time.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field, which must be protected from the effects of gravity. We demonstrate that a certain upper limit on the gravitational disruption of global symmetries would be required for this model to be consistent with the observed CMB data. Such a bound would have far-reaching implications, influencing the behavior of both particle physics and gravitational waves.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations from the AstroSat mission of the globular cluster NGC 4147. These observations were released in 2016 and 2017. The FUV spectrum, measured with the UltraViolet Imaging Telescope, has allowed us to identify 32 hot stars within the cluster. The 10 brightest stars were further analyzed to derive effective temperatures, luminosities, and internal ages using the 2009 Gaia photometry. The obtained ages ranged from 1.5 to 3.1 gyr, indicating that the cluster has entered the globular cluster blue hook phase. The temperature and luminosity patterns match those of another older cluster, NGC 4833, validating our findings and the UV IT detector's reliability. Multiple sequence patterns observed may be the result of various underlying mechanisms such as first generation blue subgiant evolution, horizontal branch noise, or noise in the Gaia measurements. Potential candidates for first generation blue subgiant evolution are also explored.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, and this new application is a direct generalization of the existing b-principle cases of oriented submersions and open maps.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability allows DNNs to leverage their previous knowledge when tackling new tasks, much like specialists becoming general practitioners and utilizing acquired expertise to tackle novel challenges. Transfer learning is a core aspect of the deep learning paradigm and has facilitated the accelerated development and achievement of state-of-the-art outcomes in various applications. Two widely-held assumptions regarding transferability have been extensively researched: the theory claiming similar features yield greater transferability, and the idea suggesting similar tasks yield greater transferability. However, numerical investigations conducted across multiple datasets and networks contradict these two theories. These findings raise questions regarding the reliability of transferability heuristics and highlight the importance of applying a principled approach when designing transfer learning strategies for achieving better empirical results.

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examination of massive diffusion processes, the precise mechanisms influencing informational and social waves remains unclear, particularly at the individual level. Our research reveals that the inherent structure of networks acts as the primary driver governing the speed of information and social behavior diffusion. Moreover, the outcomes are influenced predominantly by the early stages of the diffusion process, with superlinear growth often leading to faster averages. Notably, the rate of information diffusion can increase exponentially with a finite amount of participating agents. Consequently, the present findings provide a fundamental framework for the design of various applications, such as viral marketing and community emergence, by leveraging network dynamics.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive uniqueness proof for special Lagrangians and a detailed criterion describing the process by which a collection of varifolds converges towards a special Lagrangian, with this criterion itself dependent on Lagrangian angles.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study aims to explore this type of attack that often receives insufficient attention due to a lack of knowledge about the Android ecosystem or a focus on general evasion attacks. The study will examine the characteristics of problem-space evasion attacks, utilizing a novel taxonomy that examines the key elements of each attack type, including the hacker's profile, mode of operation, and the impact assessment of compromised apps.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. However, achieving consistency and correctness in applications relies heavily on the underlying infrastructure's design. This is especially true when handling sequential tasks, which necessitate complex resource and dependency management. In traditional approaches, designing and orchestrating services involves a significant amount of low-level coding and repetitive work, making it difficult to implement concurrent tasks and achieve resource efficiency. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a universal orchestration framework, denoted as Ozy, which enables the task configuration through a JSON file and automates the scheduling and dependency resolution for the complex tasks. Furthermore, Ozy allows users to plug in their own strategies for handling exceptions and managing resources, providing a highly customizable solution. Our experiments on various task sets have demonstrated Ozy's effectiveness in consolidating multiple tasks into smaller code snippets and enhancing concurrency, resulting in O(N) improved execution times.

Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by a reoccurring phase of unusual quantized nature, which is gapped in the thermodynamic limit.  Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase exhibits distinct topological characteristics by hosting a set of unique full pseudospin degeneracies that are separated by nonzero low-energy fluxes at zero and finite Landau levels mixing.  A variational wave function developed for this unique phase of matter is found to surpass the existing ones in terms of performance in the intermediate mixing strength range.  Additionally, this unique phase of matter is host to a set of unusual low-energy collective excitations including a non-bosonic composite fermion with non-zero Chern number, a non-abelian non-composite fermion, a non-abelian vorticity of the composite fermion, a non-abelian particle-hole dual of the composite fermion, all of which are found to be non-abelian in nature.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single black hole feeding on non-interacting isotropic dust throughout the entire universe since its inception, which is contradicted by the current cosmological consensus. Furthermore, the process specified would result in the rapid disappearance of a significant number of black holes. Unlike the Radio Galaxy model, which draws matter from surrounding galaxies, the Thakurta metric does not offer any mechanism for continuous mass accumulation. As a result, the parameters associated with this model would rapidly approach the singularity, making it incompatible with the observed characteristics of individual supermassive black holes. The bounds derived by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration on primordial black holes remain unaltered, as they are unchanged due to a lack of evidence supporting the existence of such black holes in the given range of masses.

The complexity of gaps and ring formations in protoplanetary discs indicates pressure hotspots connected to ongoing planet formation and other factors, with hydrodynamic models predicting widespread presence of ring-like dust structures in these discs. Recent studies suggest that dust rings can facilitate planet formation, and our research aims to investigate how disc hotspots affect this process. We ran simulations of a hot spot in a disc where a planet forms typical characteristics, including accretion, accretion-induced migration, and interactions between a planet and dust grains. We used higher-order models to account for the spatial extent of the disc's pressure gradient and found that a planet formed more quickly in the disc's inner region. This result implies that a planet could form rapidly in a hot spot due to increased pebble accretion, and our research indicates an approximate time frame of 0.3-0.5 million years for this process within a hot spot of a typical disc density. Moreover, our simulations show that a planet's type and the disc's structure may influence its migration pattern, and further investigations are required to determine if hydrodynamic effects shape a planet's orbital elements during early formation.

Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be a result of computational limitations inherent to the problems we're trying to solve, rather than characteristics of the data and our objectives. We demonstrate that having ample model parameters isn't necessarily necessary for achieving optimal performance when processing certain types of tasks using computers with limited computational capacity. Specifically, we find that using algorithms that can be described using polynomial equations in relation to model parameters can overcome the constraints on available computer memory and running time. Moreover, such polynomial descriptions can lead to theoretical guarantees similar to those obtained by regularized learning theories. To reinforce this concept, we provide two examples: one involving learning to accurately approximate a function with a neural network where the number of operations is constrained, and another related to predicting binary classifications under a limited character limit. These examples illustrate how varying the model parameters' growth rate (both in terms of the number of parameters and parameter sizes) can result in significant differences in performance.

Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in two-prime sumsets have been proven. More specifically, considering a countable discrete abelian group $G$ of finite type, it has been proven that any $3$-prime sumset containing a Bohr set is, in fact, an expansive set. Furthermore, this holds true with the additional constraint that the summands' frequency spectrum within the Bohr set have maximum multiplicity of $1$. Additionally, it has been proven that expansive sets are prevalent among $3$-prime sumsets of groups of finite type. In the spirit of Poltoratskii's theorem for $\mathbb{Z}^d$, it has been consistently proven that for any countable discrete group $G$ of finite type, the sumset of its Bohr sets corresponding to prime frequencies is expansive. This Bohr set is not only expansive but also has a frequency spectrum of unit multiplicity. This result's uniqueness was demonstrated through a counterexample of its reversibility. Ultimately, it has been proven that no finite set of primes can jointly produce an expansive sumset if the group $G$ is of finite type but features prime factors less than the square root of $2$. This outcome was verified to be consonant with MacIntyre's recently developed countable group generalization of Poltoratskii's Freiman's 8-theorem.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and ten vehicles, revealing that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding significantly more optimal solutions and tighter bounds.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product information tasks in e-commerce, focusing on visual and textual modalities. We introduce KMP-E-commerce, a large, publicly available dataset incorporating domain-specific knowledge for multi-modal pretraining. The KMP-E-commerce dataset features 125,000 labeled samples with detailed product annotations, enabling effective modalities interaction and task-oriented learning. Based on this dataset, we develop ELS-DAPPO, a novel pre-trained model that incorporates knowledge-based attention and latent structure for multi-modal pretraining. The ELS-DAPPO model significantly outperforms existing alternatives in selling point extraction and product information search tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of large-scale pretraining with structured knowledge for e-commerce applications.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, allowing for the reduction of data complexity and the discovery of meaningful patterns. Nevertheless, few existing methods apply siamese unsupervised learning techniques, which investigate differences between individual data points, to longitudinal cognitive anatomy data. Our focus is on further developing an unsupervised approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), to distinguish between healthy and affected groups, as well as Lord-Fisher divergence, to measure temporal feature changes and detect longitudinal patterns. Our experiment involves grouping normal control, early dementia, and mild vascular dementia subjects based on MRI scans of brain structure, and testing DIM's ability to identify feature distinctions and separate the groups over time. Our results show that DIM successfully distinguishes between the three groups when working with data from a single time period and also detects changes in cognitive function over time. Interestingly, DIM's feature extraction capabilities surpass those of Lord-Fisher divergence. Our findings suggest that DIM could efficiently detect early-stage dementia and track cognitive deterioration over time, presenting promising prospects for further research.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an efficient search algorithm termed Backward Dropping Algorithm, and an innovative feature engineering technique known as the "dagger technique". Firstly, the paper introduces I-score, an innovative score that identifies and prioritizes crucial linguistic semantics for accurate text classification predictions. Subsequently, the paper suggests using Backward Dropping Algorithm to manage dependencies within large datasets. Additionally, the paper proposes "dagger technique" which ensures an optimal association between the input variables and target variable. These methods can be applied universally across feed-forward ANNs, CNNs, and GNNs, as demonstrated through their application in predicting depression symptoms using fastText features from social media. Our best-performing model, employing an interaction-based recurrent neural network, achieved superior results to existing methods, with an error rate reduction of 6.58%.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ represents the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Increasing interactions within this phase causes a shift to a state resembling a spin-orbit coupled lattice, characterized by sublattice 90-degree rotational symmetry. Additionally, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ increases with magnetic fields, up to a saturated value, independent of electron interactions. We observe a decrease in $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ under high inter-sublattice interaction but note that this effect can be mitigated by inter-orbital interaction, which introduces a transfer of electrons between orbitals.

A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal symmetry breakdown in the dark sector. This phenomenon can only occur
at a scale separate from the typical conformal symmetry scale. The proposed
dark matter model involves a scalar field connected to a non-linear sigma model
over a symmetric space, specifically the CP^k-1 manifold, which yields an
attractive potential for this field. The existence of an unstable state within
the sigma model's spectrum creates a decay pathway for dark matter, resulting
instability, which is counteracted by a potential unified dark matter annihilation
mechanism through a hidden U(1) group under which all matter, including the
astrophysical scale dark matter, becomes charged. Consequently, this model can
satisfy both cosmic structure and relic abundance demands while generating a
potential explanation for the (g-2)_mu anomaly. Additionally, this model can
potentially resolve the Smallest Amount Problem in Dark Matter, a hitherto
unaddressed inquiry.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, accurately assessing their performance in varying scenarios is crucial. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original data source. This "black-box" model assessment technique is based on conformal prediction and is being evaluated across various medical image datasets and distribution shift scenarios, such as changes in medical institution, imaging technology, or clinical settings. By promoting more effective evaluation methods for AI models, we hope to standardize assessments, promote reliability, and provide comparative insights across studies.

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic-level details are now being extensively employed to study nucleic acid structures due to their high precision and resolution in space and time. While this high precision is advantageous, it often results in a computationally demanding process. In simulations conducted over specific timeframes, nucleic acids exhibit minor changes while conformations are largely unchanged, but their rotation and translation show little response to the temperature. To rectify this issue, the DNA structure is being constrained using fixed parameters, and then, based on those constraints, an enhanced sampling technique is used to increase the likelihood of higher precision conformations. Following the constraints, the DNA model enters a dynamic state where harmonic constraints are gradually loosened, enabling the adoption of more probable and higher precision conformations. Our method is successful in increasing the density of visited states, resulting in better distribution and statistics of nucleic acid conformations without altering the DNA's intrinsic characteristics, such as melting temperature, at significantly lower computational costs.

For optical communication systems using amplitude-shift modulation (ASM), the research community has been debating the efficiency of arithmetic to decimal conversion methods like arithmetic to fractional and binary conversion. A new approach presented in this paper converts the amplitude values of a signal into a binary expression using a variable bit length based on its magnitude. Simulation results indicate that this approach can provide bit savings of up to 2 bits per sample when the signal has a low noise level, and remains consistent with the bit error rate requirements of the communication standard. When the signal has higher noise levels, the bit savings can still range from 0.8 to 1.2 bits per sample. The proposed technique offers simplified implementation and reduced power consumption which could be useful for applications requiring high speed data conversion.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and presence of liquid phases. Electrolyte dielectric behavior is influenced in a complex manner by ion-water and ion-ion interactions, and this phenomenon's intricacies can be better understood with knowledge of respective concentrations. The cement paste's pore solution exhibits a dielectric behavior transitioning from a typical electrolyte pattern to that of water as it becomes more diluted. Multiscale numerical models using the Lattice Boltzmann method revealed detailed dielectric constant distributions for various concentrations, and a simplified, mathematically representable relation was established for the dielectric constant based on the cement paste's liquid phase composition and temperature.

In our earlier work, the range of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules was determined, and a predictive model based on resonance saturation was established. This model has been successful in explaining several observed hadronic molecules such as $X(3872)$, $Y(4260)$, and the $P_c$ states, and its predictions for heavy-heavy hadronic molecules seem even more likely. The fact that heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules with experimental evidence can be described by the same dominant dominant interaction, implies that heavy-heavy ones also exist naturally. Among our predictions, $T_{u,u}$, a $\bar D^0 D^0 D^0 D^0$ molecule, is particularly significant as it could account for the $T_{u,u}$ state claimed by BESIII without conflict. Moreover, our analysis for heavy-heavy molecules has also led to several novel predictions and potential observables which could be searched for by forthcoming experiments such as PANDA, BESIII, Belle II, and the LHCb.

Research on military drones is growing globally, with a focus on their swarm systems which can be used in various military applications. This study involves collecting and analyzing relevant documents from the internet, including research papers and commercial literature, to understand the underlying structures and driving factors of military drone development. By leveraging Natural Language Processing techniques, our research examines word distributions and topical relationships within this context. Our findings reveal that military drone development is driven by technological advancements and security concerns, with a strong emphasis on research development as a driving factor. This knowledge allows us to gain insights into the strategic directions and priorities of military drone development without access to additional, restricted information.

When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results to the conventional method. Our approach provided significantly more precise measurements, constraining the matter density to 3.5% and outperforming the conventional BAO method. Our study showed that the additional information, except for the spectral index constraint, came primarily from two distinct effects: the Alcock-Paczy\'nski effect and redshift space distortion.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight.

A fundamental component of various technologies, including surveillance, robotic navigation, and self-driving systems, is pedestrian trajectory prediction, and significant advancements have been made in this field. Nevertheless, past studies still have several shortcomings. The primary issues are that predicted trajectories tend to deviate from their actual paths, resulting in larger offsets beyond 5s into the future; and predicted trajectories often fail to accurately account for social awareness. In response to these shortcomings, we introduce a novel trajectory prediction approach called TS3PR. This method involves leveraging a sophisticated conditional variational autoencoder framework that incorporates time-varying socially-aware recurrent networks. By leveraging time-varying socially-aware recurrent networks, our approach aims to improve the accuracy of trajectory predictions by accounting for past movements and incorporating socially-aware factors such as age, sex, and lane occupancy. Moreover, we propose the use of socially-aware visually-sensitive policy capture. This captures the socially-aware factor's impact on past trajectories. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through rigorous experiments on a large dataset, and through fair and comprehensive evaluations, we compare TS3VPc with other top-ranked prediction methods.

Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine architecture is employed as a reference point to analyze how system complexity evolves in response to variations in network dynamics and parameters. Furthermore, a variant of an information-based measure of complexity is applied to examine the process of incremental Hebbian learning in a simple associative memory network.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a series of hand gestures that instruct different swarm behaviors, was successfully implemented with three Turtlebot3 robots. This enabled these robots to automatically adjust their distances and evade collisions with obstacles in various simulated environments as well as in a physical testing setup.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. However, determining this potential requires the full Hamiltonian, posing a significant challenge for complex many-body systems. A recent approach, proposed by P. W. Claeys et al., utilizes an approximated, variational gauge potential. In the case of a two-component fermionic Hubbard model, this potential can be expressed using nested commutators. A critical insight in this context reveals that optimizing the variational parameters leads to a set of linear equations, whose coefficients are determined by these commutators. As a proof of this model's applicability, the method is used to develop an efficient driving scheme for preparing the ground state of a cluster molecule. Additionally, the method is capable of driving the system from a local maximum to the ground state by simply adjusting the sign of the corresponding term in the equations.

Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale counterparts. In this study, a streamlined, fast image decolorization approach based on color temperature perception is developed. The aberration occurring in color perception is a result of light's varying refractive indices depending on wavelength and angle of incidence, resulting in the illusion of color. The proposed lich method utilizes a color space, fragments it into its component channels, performs pixel-wise operations, and applies Hermite interpolation for efficient and optimized results. The aim of this method is to yield high-quality color images in an expedited manner while maintaining fidelity to the original tone mapped grayscale image. The underlying idea behind this approach involves identifying and categorizing pixels into three groups: those that can maintain their color details, those that lose their lich details but retain their color, and those that experience lich detail loss along with color loss. The method employs three distinct strategies for each category of pixels to achieve enhanced results. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that the lich method achieves high-quality color images in an expedited time, and surpasses existing techniques in terms of both visual quality and time efficiency. The underlying source code for lich has been shared publicly on https://github.com/imcasPE/liceFast.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequent applications of these results enable the computation of certain infinite series connected to Stirling numbers.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2.

We've created a state-of-the-art laser-plasma platform to study fundamental photon-photon collision phenomena, such as the linear Breit-Wheeler process using real photons, by leveraging the Gemini laser facility at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory. The platform employs a high-powered laser wakefield accelerator and bremsstrahlung radiation to generate high-intensity photon beams colliding with kiloelectronvolt plasmon photons. To track possible particle creation in the collision, we've developed a custom-made magnetic field and set up particle detection systems, including electron and anti-electron detectors, to record potential pair creation events. To validate our approach and ensure its applicability to a wider range of scientific applications, we've demonstrated the effective use of plasma focus devices or laser plasma interactions to generate high-energy electron beams. Additionally, we're exploring methods to achieve nonlinear photon-photon collisions through the interaction of relativistic electrons in a laser-plasma focus setup, aiming to observe signatures of photon-photon collisions similar to the SM Higgs boson or other particle phenomena.

In a scenario where a second Higgs doublet has a high energy value, a number of predictions can be re-evaluated. Theoretical concepts, such as relationships between various bosons and a distinct signature involving opposite-sign charged leptons, are examined in relation to the second Higgs doublet's energy and a specific parameter within the $Z_2$ symmetry. The impact of the second Higgs doublet's energy on these predictions changes significantly as the specific parameter approaches certain thresholds. In addition to these predictions, constraints are also placed on the second Higgs doublet's energy based on the existence of charged Higgs bosons within existing particle collision data. The predictions' feasibility is then assessed under the constraints of various distinct models such as the alignment limit and a specific scenario where naturalness is preserved.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to create the target schema's IRIs and introduce constraints for the source data. Using this approach, we devise a catalog-based method that ensures compliance with the canonical solution property. Additionally, we leverage linear programming to generate the canonical solution, also specifying the data exchange problems' LP formulation.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now bridge a significant knowledge gap in this field. The application of these techniques has been hindered due to significant computational requirements and lack of a comprehensive and open-access software solution. The Python package 'pyStoNED' aims to address this challenge by offering a user-friendly toolset that unifies advanced optimization algorithms to support novel methods and classical techniques, thereby enabling easy implementation. The package provides detailed implementation guides and showcases method comparisons and real-world examples.

This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for examining the lower mass spectrum resulting from top-quark pairs produced in association with a neutral, scalar particle ($\phi$). Our approach, which can be applied to the HL-LHC with existing data from the LHC, does not require prior understanding of the $\phi$ coupling to top-quarks and leptons. Even with the limitations of the 13 TeV LHC data, our method can be used to establish exclusion limits on $\phi$ mass below 10 GeV/c$^2$. Furthermore, this technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of scenarios beyond the simple scalar model, providing valuable insights into the underlying physics. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that a 13 TeV LHC with 300 inverse femtobarns of input can rule out the pure Higgsino PMSSM-8 scenario up to the Landau pole mass of 37.5 TeV. Our initial results also indicate that a 27 TeV HL-LHC with 360 inverse femtobarns of input can rule out the bulk gravity region of the model up to a gravity scale of 6.4 TeV.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two primary contributions: first, it establishes that incorporating a single step of fine-tuning enables efficient achievement of high accuracy in unsupervised parsing without needing to construct pre-requisites like constituent segmentation; second, it demonstrates that techniques like cross-domain transfer and multi-task learning can enhance parsing effectiveness in limited-data scenarios, as exemplified by the utilization of mBERT in untied, unsupervised, and few-shot parsing contexts.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for languages other than English severely hampers progress in these fields. To fill this void, we utilize Kaldi to develop German acoustic models utilizing datasets under a Creative Commons license. This has the added benefit of making these models redistributable and significantly lowering the barriers for researchers and developers in German ASR. With a combined total of 2,716 hours of audio data, the integration of raw wave files and synthesis into a single model surpasses that of English ASR. As a result, the relative error rates of spoken dialogue, public speech, and publicly available speech decrease by 14%, 12%, and 12% respectively compared to the current best-in-class models.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 V101 and 103 narrowband images from Hubble/WISExom, we have observed transformations from H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ emission balances in 30 Doradus's Be-type stars. By analyzing these changes, we discovered a distinct subset of 7 Be-type stars exhibiting secondary peaks in H$\alpha$ emissions. These stars, specifically HIP112311, HIP83646, and three HIP83669 members along with V39 Menz, have comparable Balmer emissions and spectral shifts to B-type Be-type stars found in local star clusters, indicating they are B-type B-eclipse stars. This distinction has implications on low-mass B-eclipse stars as these B-eclipse stars possess faster rotational velocities at younger ages before increasing in velocity once they become A-eclipse stars, which is less common in observed men. Furthermore, a secondary H$\alpha$ emission was detected in one B-eclipse star HIP83669, indicating an excretion disk from a companion. The sample of B-eclipse stars matches the expected binary origin of approximately 10-50% of Be-type stars in accordance with prior research, which is consistent with a 20% return rate of B-type B-eclipse stars transitioning into A-eclipse stars through orbital mergers, thereby decreasing available Be-type stars over 5 billion years. The data also shows an increased presence of

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is utilized.
Existing ITN techniques, whether rule-based or neural modeling approaches, often
involve complicated annotations and data preparation, including the need for costly,
domain-specific, high-quality training examples. In contrast, our proposed data
enhancement technique efficiently creates large amounts of accurate spoken-written
pairs from unrelated texts with minimal manual annotation. Furthermore, our
technique's effectiveness has been experimentally validated by significantly
outperforming traditional methods in various numerical formats such as integers,
currency values, and fractional numbers with a substantial accuracy boost of 14.44%.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance learning capabilities similar to Deep Neural Networks, we've developed NFTK - a neural tangent kernel based on non-fungible tangent kernels - which yields impressive results on 14 datasets. Additionally, our study indicates that NTK kernels outperform traditional kernels in most cases, and and even exhibits tangent kernel properties in certain scenarios.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a mystery. We've made a significant breakthrough in understanding the correlation-driven reduction of one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological systems. Through an in-depth analysis, we discovered a previously unknown class of correlated topological systems, distinguished by the node's susceptibility to interactions. Our research reveals that, when correlations are strong, the reduced system topology exhibits either a trivial or second-order topological characteristics. We've further observed that zero-dimensional correlated topological systems can be obtained in the reduced effective one-dimensional system from a barbic chain, yielding a different classification basis for non-Hermitian topology than previously thought.

Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation in the desired characteristics. We've specifically examined the potential of spectral flux, F1 mean, F2 mean, and their combinations in fostering warmth in female speech and the impact of voiced slope, spectral flux, and their combinations in projecting competence in female speech within synthetic voices. We've successfully integrated the essential acoustic features into existing TTS systems, leading to a notable improvement in the perception of warm and competent speech. We've also included a rating of naturalness in the experiment, as our previous study used a single-list continuous scale, but we've switched to a dual-scale approach to separate trait-specific perception from overall naturalness. We believe this approach allows for a more precise assessment of the TTS system's performance from the perspective of a human speech perceptron.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating modular A4 symmetry is proposed, where dark matter is stabilized due to both symmetry-breaking and gauge symmetry involved. The symmetry framework utilizes two modular groups, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_4$, allowing for the introduction of three zero-scale neutrino masses. However, this approach necessitates high-scale A4 symmetry breaking via the scalar field $\sigma$, where its fiducial value is set at the GUT scale. Consequently, dark matter stability is further ensured by the combination of symmetry-breaking and gauge symmetry involved. The former originates from the modular weight of the standard model fermions, while the latter is certain $n$ in the term $(3H^\dota)^4 \cos(4\varphi_\sigma)$ influencing dark matter stability, where $H^\dota$ is a transverse component of the scalar field $\sigma$. Furthermore, introducing non-holonomic terms and gauging the U(1)_(B-L) symmetry, which influences the relic density of dark matter, result in the introduction of a massive gauge boson beyond the electroweak scale for dark matter annihilation through the Higgs mechanism.

Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By combining deformed canonical commutation relations with the Pauli-Podolsky prescription, a quantized Hamiltonian operator for triaxial nuclei is derived and solved. Results indicate a new collective parameter arises from the angular part of the quadrupole operator, related to the minimal length, which separates collective and non-collective motions. We found the minimal length affects not only the collective vibrations but also the peaking effect in the rotor states and introduces a new discrete spectrum in the rotational excitations. Moreover, the minimal length couples with the axis rotation, which led to revised rotational band structures.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the difficulties in analyzing vast datasets of multi-spectral images captured at various time points. This work introduces a cutting-edge approach that integrates time series analysis and deep learning, utilizing a Fusion Deep Convolutional Autoencoder for unsupervised anomaly detection in long-term, high-resolution hyperspectral imaging. By fusing visual and spectral data, a new FCVA model leverages both forms of information to produce meaningful change maps. Our method demonstrates superior performance on the Pavia University dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques including spectral clustering and local Fisher discriminant analysis.

A comprehensive study investigates the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was found to be limited, yet adjusting the density can successfully relate the viscosity of non-associated fluids to idealized models. Consequently, this comparison generates a length that directly relates to the liquid's cubic root volume.

The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, driven by vacuum expansion during the Syrian Era, followed by matter domination and acceleration in the De Sitter Era, has been suggested. Both phases are predicted by standard Lambda Cold Dark Matter models, yet these phenomena have distinct implications for the sizes of periodic and late-time voids. While the early era sets the initial conditions for structure formation, the late-era voids compete with the existing matter-based voids formed during the Syrian Era. This results in the emergence of peculiar shapes and stress patterns. We investigate the characteristics of these inter-era voids and their effects on the stress tensor of the dark matter component. Our findings indicate that the stress tensor of these inter-era voids can exceed their matter density density within several comoving cycles, leading to the disappearance of these voids only when the late-era voids dominate the matter density of the universe.

The invariant-set theory, a superdeterministic approach to addressing the cosmological constant problem and the quantum measurement paradox, is being examined within a hidden-variable framework. Initially, we establish a predictive model grounded in the framework and demonstrate that it fails to meet the criterion of local realism. Subsequently, we proceed with an in-depth analysis of a modified version of this model, one that enables predictions in line with local realism, with the caveat that this likely comes at the expense of consistency with established physical principles.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage.

In the case where lattice spacing vanishes, the dimer model's critical properties align with those of 2D fermions coupled with a gauge field.  In order to derive the effective action for the gauge field from this setup, diagrammatic expansion needs to be performed within a framework that accounts for the propagator's response to external photons.  Building on the statistical mechanics approach developed by Kekez and one of the present authors, a method for computing the dimer Green's function in the presence of a gauge field was established, which can be applied to 2D fermions as well.  In the context of 2D fermions, this method was used to establish a connection between the diagrammatic expansion of the propagator and the spectral dimension.  In addition, an algorithm for computing gauge field correlations was also developed, which can be applied to 2D fermions as well.  In order to test the efficacy of these methods, they were applied to the study of 2D fermions in a background unitary gauge field with a random component.  Specifically, the method was used to compute the diffusion constant, the spectral dimension, and the scaling of the Yang-Mills action.  In addition, it was verified that the method yields results consistent with perturbative renormalization group calculations.  Furthermore, a comparison with numerical simulations revealed that the method accurately captures the non-perturbative physics of the Yang-Mills action.
