Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly challenging as the number of variables grows, as it often requires implementing specific algorithms or utilizing hard constraints, contrary to handling continuous variables where the "all dims given" approach can be employed. Recently, a condition was established to ensure sparse groups from the Group Lasso that can be applied to categorical data under the Sinkhorn stability condition. In this study, a comparison of model selection criteria and conditions is made, leading to derived sufficient conditions for sparse group recovery and more accessible techniques for selecting models along with a proposed criterion, all aimed at facilitating high-dimensional categorical data analysis through sparse modeling and group selection.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, long-term performance but also the capability to efficiently handle security issues after malicious programs have been installed, for instance, to safeguard intellectual property.  To address the first concern, developers utilized the concept of partitioning to create separate areas of a system's resources.  However, this approach did not adequately meet the second requirement due to the additional complexities involved in its implementation.

A more effective solution has been developed - virtualization.  This approach creates a platform-independent interface between software and hardware, enabling the separation of the system's control mechanisms and its physical assets.  As a result, it becomes possible to leverage general-purpose operating systems that can provide integrated network services, thus facilitating the development and deployment of embedded systems.

Embodied in a hypervisor, this concept functions as a bridge between software and hardware, fording the path to integration with existing embedded systems.  To address the performance issues, researchers have recently turned to the support of virtualization provided by modern processors.

In this paper, a hypervisor, named T-Visor, is proposed and its functionality, design, and testing are presented.  Built upon the seL4 security-oriented micro-hypervisor, T-Visor serves as a general-purpose hypervisor, capable of supporting both security integration and long-term system performance.  As a comprehensive case study, the development process of T-Visor has been documented, providing

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel approaches to stitching panoramic images with a single row of cameras have been developed, starting with the rotation matrix that accounts for camera orientation. By simplifying the stitching problem, existing solutions such as Planar Guided Image Stitching have been improved upon, resulting in the development of new methods including Multi View Matching and Homography. These methods demonstrate superior performance in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy in aligning images. Furthermore, the proposed methods enable more precise calculation of the camera rotation angle, known as omega, by leveraging the prior knowledge of camera orientation. These approaches also introduce the integration of omega into the Universal Homography Estimator, thereby enhancing the estimator's accuracy in aligning images. Experimental results across various platforms have confirmed the proposed methods outperform Planar Guided Image Stitching in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

When two identical populations with local interactions are coupled, the population dynamics can evolve into a chimeric state even with heterogeneous reaction parameters that affect the system's initial condition. The emergence of this phenomenon is tied to a non-trivial transition in the algebraic structure of the system's invariant manifold. Specifically, when coupling occurs, a new chimeric equilibrium arises, and further, dynamic systems with uniformly distributed parameter heterogeneity in both populations can also yield this equilibrium, and, consequently, chimeras. Furthermore, one population can drive a Hopf bifurcation in the other, resulting in the emergence of chimera states through phase locking transitions. The presented analysis employs a mathematical framework applicable to a broad range of coupled systems, and it highlights the distinct role of parameter heterogeneity within this framework.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, are susceptible to the same limitations as other learning controllers, specifically their lack of robustness to slight changes in the environment's dynamics and policies. Our research demonstrates that the model-based Reinforcement Learning method, Probabilistic Policy Optimization, has the potential to learn a policy that is stable under slight environmental variations. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for this robustness and through simulations on multiple environments that model transitions and dynamics through probabilistic distributions, validate the effectiveness of this approach, even when the initial model is inaccurate.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it allows us to categorize these higher dimension algebras up to equivalence using their fundamental properties and arrangement of components.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, a similar duality is demonstrated using random tensor networks.  By examining individual tensors, non-trivial effects are discovered that resolve discrepancies at the page phase transition.  By aggregating these effects, the reflected entanglement spectrum is derived analytically and aligns with numerical findings, providing a framework for resolving order of limits issues.  Applying this approach to hyperbolic networks yields results consistent with holographic predictions.  Furthermore, a distinct entanglement structure and a non-flat R\'enyi spectrum are observed, revealing various sector-like contributions.  It's hypothesized that these distinct sectors arise from a representation of the canonical partition function as a sum of independent sub-systems.

Modelling heritable data in continuous-time Markov chains is often tackled by state space partitioning. However, existing approaches have limitations, particularly for large and complex systems. Research on persistent stochastic dynamics has shed light on the concepts of recurrence and randomness, which we'll draw upon to introduce a new approach. This method utilizes a pattern's characteristic time scale to calculate its duration between appearances, determined by the inverse of an object's relaxation time. We've developed an algorithm for evaluating this time, which we've demonstrated to be conservative, particularly for patterns that follow exponential decay. We've also discovered that, contrary to expectations, persistent dynamics can occur in both random and recurrent cases, as seen in patterns that exhibit transient behavior but with a finite expectation of persistence. We've presented different scenarios of permanent data preservation and provided conditions under which our algorithm is efficient, providing a new strategy for modeling heritable data and uncovering pattern longevity in stochastic systems.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. A thorough analysis of the existence of attractors in these systems reveals that they can have either a point, saddle-focus or saddle type. We thoroughly explore the conditions required for the emergence of these attractors, taking into account parameter values and initial state preferences. Ultimately, our research identifies preferred regions for the initial state in the 3D phase space that are more suitable for the attraction of these systems.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept, describing how solutions to certain gravitational equations are derived from corresponding gauge theories through a process of reduction. This study investigates a different theoretical connection with a view to applying it to quantum gravity, focusing on data encoding a loop's gravitational properties. It is found that, like the double copy, information on the gravitational properties of a loop can be independently reduced from both Yang-Mills theory and a special kind of topological field theory. This separate relationship, referred to as the single copy, is defined against the background of a fixed, stationary spacetime loop. Furthermore, theoretical tools including the Valence restriction and restrictions of the BH symmetry and CS reduction are employed to confirm that the gravitational properties of loops remain unaffected under certain transformations. This study also reveals that, unlike the double copy, this separate relationship, known as the single copy, is not invariant to certain transformations and thus necessitates an adjustment if it is to be applied to quantum gravity. This study also outlines a different approach to computing the properties of loops, known as the discrete path-AMM map.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining how
the number of hook lengths divisible by $t$ in the partitions of $n$ varies.
The support of the resulting distribution, $Y_t(n)$, diminishes significantly
as $t$ increases (specifically, for $t=3$), leading to the conclusion that the
only distribution it satisfies is the zero function. Ultimately, this research resolves
a portion of Combinatorical Challenge 12.11 posed by George Andrews and Herbert
S. Wilf, and also confirms an unsolved case from the book "Partitions and Determinants"
by Ian Ady, which had previously proven elusive to him and Michael Chapman.

This investigation leverages the Jacobi-Trudi identity and the Pl\"uckering relations,
while also discovering an additional relationship involving the Schur functions that may
have potential for additional applications.

Measuring the quantum tunneling rate of particles through a potential barrier has been done using Larmor clocks in which the tunneling probability is described using the Larmor angle. This paper begins with a heuristic derivation of the tunnel problem that defines the Larmor time independently of the Larmor angle. It then presents a more direct method for which the Larmor angle vanishes, revealing that the rate of tunneling is dictated by the average value of the square of the Larmor angle over a specific time frame. This, in turn, is associated with fluctuations in the effective lifetime of a tunneling particle. Consequently, the average Larmor time can be utilized for identifying the tunneling time. Two models, quadratic and asymptotic tunnel barriers, are then investigated to determine the tunneling time under these conditions. Ultimately, the proposed approach is deemed suitable for developing novel quantum technologies.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function, irrespective of the specific type of meson. A light-cone QCD sum rule approach is employed to derive the amplitude's normalization and the associated Lattice QCD calculation, previously conducted by Dragos et al. (Phys.Rev.D 97 (2018) 054034), is utilized. A semiempirical expression for the universal function is introduced, combining the results of two studies - Chernyakov and Zhitnitsky (Sov.J.Nucl.Phys 27 (1978) 668) and T. Hashimoto (Phys.Lett.B 783 (2018) 137018). Our findings reveal that the P-wave amplitudes' asymptotic behavior follows a $6/z^5$ formula. Moreover, the research provides the amplitudes' normalization, $A_{(0/1)}=0.35\pm 0.09$ and $A_2=0.57\pm 0.16$, along with the corresponding moments $\langle z^k \rangle_{P_w}$ for the specified mesons. The research's estimates for the amplitudes' normalization can be brought to a more precise state by employing the results of two studies - chao-dissipative QCD lattice (

This research paper explores the possibility of implementing a quantum gate called the Hadamard gate in a specific type of system known as a nonlinear Bose-Einstein condensate. At the points where the atoms interact with one another, the behavior is driven by a complex force rather than a simple repulsive effect found in other condensates. A comprehensive study of the dynamic changes in this system over time is conducted under the assumption that the atoms move within a fixed potential shape with two distinct minima. Our findings reveal a wide range of interesting phenomena including the creation of solitons, symmetrical wave patterns, and instability leading to periodic oscillations. By analyzing the wave functions of the atoms, it becomes clear that the atom-particle interactions play a crucial role in these phenomena. Our investigation also assesses the effectiveness of these gate implementations and suggests methods for successfully implementing the Hadamard gate in this system.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate that the asymptotic symmetry algebra of null infinity is likely to be the extended BMS algebra with its phase factor removed. Additionally, this article verifies that the extended BMS algebra is indeed the one appearing in the extended Burgess or double soft theorems at the level of tree and next-to-leading calculations. Furthermore, similar findings apply to the broader class of Weinberg's infinite series for very soft factors. Also covered in this article are the properties of charges associated with drag minimization, subleading soft theorems, the application of Mellin transforms in this context, and a proposed extension of celestial holography where the extended BMS algebra appears before the Mellin product appearing in the bulk.

Learning with the entire data at once isn't a viable option due to limitations on storage and computational resources. Online methods however collect and process data sequentially but often result in representations that are not compatible. Therefore, a new approach called Neural Architecture for Online Ensemble Continual Learning (NOECAL) is proposed, gathering multiple online models and combining them into an ensemble capable of adapting to evolving distribution shifts. NOECAL redefines online models as feature extractors then fuses them into a single architecture, allowing the methods to be hybridized and analyzed. However, hybridizing requires significant computational and storage costs. Therefore, a compact version of NOECAL is also developed by fusing the outputs of these models rather than the intermediate features, resulting in a computational save of 90%. Experiments show NOECAL's performance surpasses state-of-the-art methods including Standard Online (SOCAL) in both feature extractor and classification stages, achieving a notable 10% improvement. Furthermore, NOECAL's compact version offers a 90% reduction in computational and storage requirements compared to the primary version, making it a more efficient option.

In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve first and second-type differential forms that are closely related to null connections and distinguish between conformally related metrics. This research demonstrates that Einstein's vacuum equations enable the conversion of certain null connections into Levi-Civita connections, ultimately giving rise to Ricci flat metrics. This transformation is exemplified by converting certain conformally flat metrics back into their original form.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections cause a multitude
of issues, such as physical and mental disorders, often leading to the death
of young children and immunocompromised individuals. Notwithstanding a propensity
for human diagnostic error, visual inspection is still predominantly utilized
for clinical diagnoses. Previous studies exploring the application of computer-
aided intestinal parasite classification have faced challenges due to the visual
similarities between parasites and other contaminants in fecal matter. This
paper introduces Deep Belief Networks as a solution to the challenges associated
with intestinal parasite classification, presenting classification results on a
dataset comprising fecal worm eggs and larvae, as well as stool particles. The
experimental findings indicate that the proposed method achieves a high level of
accuracy in classifying intestinal parasites while maintaining exceptional
precision for excluding negative diagnoses.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates regime-switching models featuring not only stochastic interest rate and diffusion price processes but also randomly occurring jumps. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, we initially present a dynamic programming-based solution strategy for a related value function, applicable to varied nonlinear reinsurance cost functions. Next, based on the approximation properties of certain split-type Markov processes, we devise a computational method for deriving practical numerical outcomes. Furthermore, we apply the proposed approach to two common cases, a linear reinsurance cost model corresponding to zero-sum investment and reinsurance games, and a supply chain management issue. Numerical evaluations related to an investment and reinsurance alliance are conducted to evaluate the efficacy of our approximation technique.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and noisy flight conditions. The mathematical derivation of the PIDA controller is based on a specific nonlinear flight model, and its stability is proven using the Lyapunov stability criterion. Additionally, the parameter estimation of the flight model is discussed, and a stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm is used to efficiently calculate PIDA controller gains, resulting in smooth, stable flight dynamics with minimal vibration. Furthermore, a Genetic Filter is applied to effectively eliminate noise and adaptively tune the estimation error, while also providing a measure of state accuracy and estimation error magnitude. Simulation results are presented to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed PIDA controller over traditional PID strategies, particularly under uncertain and noisy conditions.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key topics addressed include the application of chiral effective
field theory, the significance of the sigma term, an understanding of the qualitative nature
of low-energy phase shifts, the physics governing the $\Delta$ isobar, and isospin violation.
It is emphasized that pion-nucleon scattering at low energy is intrinsically connected to QCD through effective
field theory. Moreover, the need for a more detailed low-energy data set concerning the pion-nucleon sigma term
and isospin violation is underscored.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was tested, integrating eight pilot blades incorporating new technology. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained hands-on experience with the new design. This article outlines the results of these experiments and describes the associated instrumentation along with the methods employed for data analysis. Moreover, it presents pilot module performance during cosmic ray tests and offers a comparison between the new and existing designs.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to accurately identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the first billion years of the universe's existence. To do this, we employed two AI algorithms. Firstly, the PSFGAN algorithm separated the light coming from the host galaxy from the light coming from the galaxy's central source. We then used the GaMorNet algorithm to categorize the host galaxies into either disk-like, bulge-like, or indeterminate forms. We used images taken by the Subaru telescope across different colors and at three distinct stages of galaxy development. To build this system, we initially trained it on thousands of computer-simulated galaxies and then fine-tuned it using fewer images of real galaxies. Our framework's accuracy is approximately 70% for pinpointing galaxy forms and nearly 90% for estimating their brightness. We found that the proportions of disk-like, bulge-like, and indeterminate host galaxies are approximately 60%, 30%, and 10% across all redshifts. We observed a rise in the proportion of bulge-like host galaxies from 20% at redshift 0.3-0.6 to 40% at redetchift 0.6-1.0. We found that disk-like host galaxies are more common at lower redshifts than those with smaller masses but that at higher redshifts, mass is the primary factor. We found that galaxies with smaller masses have fewer bulge

We employ the Folding model using GMatrix elements, and combine it with a Monte Carlo mapping technique from the Senboku-Yong type. We introduce a new method that allows us to determine the short-range correlation distribution in phase space. This correlation distribution is represented by the second order GMatrix factor. Furthermore, we introduce the Cumulant-GMatrix mapping (CAGM) method to determine the Correlation-GMatrix factor. We compare the two methods as applied to $^{12}$C and $^{16}$C, revealing that CAGM provides a clearer identification of the correlation distribution, while simultaneously preserving the clarity of the Folding map. This suggests CAGM to be a more suitable method for studying SRCs. We also discuss how these SRCs affect the density and momentum distributions. Additionally, we discuss how these SRCs impact the nuclear phase space and geometry.

We are seeing significant advancement in complex-valued deep learning (CDL), but its core principles have not been fully explored from a mathematical standpoint that takes network complexity into consideration. A crucial aspect that requires more research involves how CDL handles the co-domain of complex numbers, specifically their relationship to geometric representations such as the phase and magnitude planes. In this paper, we investigate co-domain symmetry as a fundamental principle for CDL and identify its essential characteristics. We establish two methods to implement co-domain symmetry: a constraint approach that uses real-valued networks to promote symmetry, and a design approach that directly incorporates complex weights. We show that incorporating co-domain symmetry can improve the performance of CDL and address issues related to overfitting; incorporating geometric symmetry can provide even greater gains and reduce overfitting further.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within the saturation regime, distinctive geometrical scaling patterns arise due to the interrelated nature of gluon distribution and transverse momentum.  The occurrence of geometrical scaling in various physical processes indicates the importance of saturation.  The theoretical framework underlying these findings is based on the concept of renormalization group operators developed by J. Dasgupta and E. Gualdin.  The goal of this paper is to introduce theoretical foundations of geometrical scaling and provide comprehensive numerical data verifying the occurrence of geometrical scaling in several high-energy processes.  Furthermore, this paper presents distinct features of heavy ion collision phenomena at the LHC and future facilities like the FCC and FA.

A thorough study measured the abundance of twelve key chemical elements within eighty-six extremely metal-poor stars residing close to the Sun, focusing on their metallicities and radial velocities. Our analysis revealed that nine out of twelve elements exhibit some level of abundance variability among stars of a given metallicity level. After meticulously accounting for measurement uncertainties and potential internal mixing within these low-metallicity stars, the source of the abundance variability was determined. The results show that ten out of twelve elements have abundance values that significantly differ at the 3-sigma confidence level, while also uncovering variability among stars of different metallicity levels. Our findings reveal that metal production occurred early on in the history of the Universe, specifically between $10^{8.5}$ and $10^{10.5}$ years ago. A non-uniform distribution of gas at the time of star formation, along with significant pre-enrichment from previous generation stars, are thought to be the primary explanations for the observed abundance variability.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm utilizes a reference model that isn't affected by potential biases, allowing for an accurate calculation of bias and risk levels. The proposed method is tested on a financial literacy dataset from the OECD's Survey of Adult Skills. Results indicate a significant disparity in predictive performance between models that and don't account for financial literacy baseline levels. Furthermore, a high risk level was detected in both cases, indicating that the introduction of bias increases the error rate in predictive models by 25%.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized using gradient descent methods. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how a quantum model can exploit class separability to achieve improved performance.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept to semi-slant submanifolds and leveraging warped product structures, a more comprehensive understanding can be gained. A new classification is presented for warped product semi-slant submanifolds in almost contact metric manifolds. At the warping function's origin, specific geometries become flat and are restricted to either horizontal or vertical components. Key findings include the non-existence of vertical semi-slant submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds. Additionally, when the warping function is one at the origin, specific submanifolds can be identified, and some may contain horizontal distributions. An example is provided to illustrate the segmented nature of warped product semi-slant submanifolds.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from kilograms to metric tons and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram based on the activity gradient strength. This diagram classifies dimer configurations into three types. Notably, the dimer's response to the activity gradient depends on its orientation, with antichemotactic properties increasing and chemotactic properties decreasing as the angle between the particles widens.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed in 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike those latter states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 each display magnetoroton spectral densities with two peaks rather than one, featuring magnetorotons with a spin of 2, whose chiralities differ for the 1/4 and 2/7 states, while being identical for the 2/9 state. Our findings also reveal that magnetorotons' energies obey a certain sum rule that universally applies across the systems studied. Moreover, for the 1/4 and 2/7 states, numerical simulations predict that the spectral sum rule associated with the next-order term will also be satisfied, and both states' chiral magnetoroton spectral sums converge to the same value, indicating that this property is a general fractionally charged collective excitation characteristic. Our work includes a theoretical verification that certain sum rules can be applied to collective excitations of spin-polarized systems, and for the Landau parameters of spin-polarized systems, specifically the 1/4 state, where our numerical results for the Landau parameters show good agreement with those obtained using density-matrix renormalization group methods.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for public health systems due to the immense complexity involved. However, for networks of a certain type, the dynamics can be simplified using the characteristics of the network's geometric structure. This paper outlines a basic framework for categorizing networks into simpler, more manageably-sized components, which can be efficiently processed by public health systems. A new, related problem called the Network Core Placement issue is introduced, which aims to minimize the cost of placing core nodes within a subgraph, and an approximation algorithm is proposed. Additionally, the paper conceptually discusses various criteria for evaluating the efficiency of these categorizations, and highlights some potential applications of these techniques in managing complex epidemics.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrument noise, sky variability, and other factors, leading to model inaccuracy. When this occurs, the maximum likelihood estimator can produce biased outcomes, and one common issue is the appearance of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point source signals in CMB maps. This paper delves into the causes of this bias, and proposes a straightforward yet powerful solution to rectify it. Our approach involves breaking down point sources into their individual components and applying a spatiotemporal noise model to the data. We validate the effectiveness of this method using simulated data with known point sources, and demonstrate its ability to produce accurate results at a level comparable to that of unbiassed methods.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through experimentation. Our research involves training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task (block-stacking) and assessing various methods for overcoming referential ambiguity: achieving unambiguous teaching instructions, incorporating agent preferences into teaching instructions, and adopting goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. The experiments reveal that implementing these strategies effectively addresses referential ambiguities: a method called agent-informed teaching achieves the best results, allowing both the teacher and learner to achieve higher task completion rates despite the ambiguity.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concept of shadow state tomography to the realm of quantum channel processing, where it is applied to determine the characteristics of any quantum channel using significantly fewer measurements than traditional approach. Additionally, this study outlines the necessary tools for implementing channel shadow tomography, including a novel method to naturally extend quantum states used in previous studies. Furthermore, this study demonstrates an experiment where shadow channel tomography is employed to achieve precise measurements of channel output probabilities with nearly optimal efficiency.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) holds great potential in transforming various industries such as media, healthcare, and surveillance. To effectively deliver UAS services in a timely manner, optimizing their route planning and speed is crucial. This research introduces a new model of UAV trajectory, known as the Riemannian straight line trajectory, and develops an efficient optimization technique utilizing a general procedure called penalized trajectory optimization. The method leverages a combination of numerical optimization algorithms and differential calculus to find the optimal parameters for a diverse range of UAV applications, subject to flight time constraints and dynamic obstacles. The proposed framework is versatile, allowing it to be applied for different application times and even unsupervised autonomous flight with pre-defined objectives. To demonstrate its efficacy, the performance of the penalized optimization algorithm is evaluated under various parameter settings and compared to a traditional approach, resulting in a computational speed improvement of 10 times faster while maintaining a 3 times cost function improvement. The model and associated optimization technique have the potential to be widely applied across various UAS applications.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. As a result, the system exhibits instability towards forming density-wave order compared to its counterpart in the single-layer case. Using the RG method, we investigate the competition between this instability and the possibility of forming a superconducting state. We discover that the two correlations have similar properties when comparing them to their counterparts in the single-layer case, while their interplay displays a contrasting behavior. Furthermore, we investigate the effect of bilayer couplings on these instabilities and show that, when bilayer couplings are strong, the corresponding wave vectors for both density-waves and superconductivity do not change; however, their responses to bilayer couplings vary differently.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the presence of an electric and a magnetic dipole moment. As a result, the adsorption of this molecule on a substrate changes the work function, thereby qualifying the system as magnetoelectric. Research conducted on a monolayer of Sc2TbN@C80 on h-BN/Ni(111) found that the molecules form a hexagonal unit cell with the substrate, but with a distortion due to the magnetic Tb atom pointing towards a neighboring Ni atom. However, at low temperatures, the Tb atom points towards a nearest Ni atom resulting in a larger unit cell, with a work function consistent with a ferromagnetic state. Upon thermal excitation, the Tb atom however rotates to face a neighboring molecule without touching any Ni atom, pointing towards a paramagnetic state. This new conformation leads to a smaller unit cell and a reduced work function, but initial experimental results suggest that the work function's temperature dependence is not caused by the magnetoelectric properties but rather by the general trend seen in carbon fullerene monolayers on this substrate. Nonetheless, the observed change in work function's temperature behavior could be an indication of thermal motion influencing properties at the quantum point.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings, which this communication seeks to summarize. A survey reveals that the majority of lightweight algorithms trade off security for efficiency, specifically using reduced-precision arithmetic, simplified key generation processes, or infrequent updating of keys. We explore various lightweight encryption techniques, discuss their core features, and assess their applicability to IoT settings, focusing on encryption methods employing hash functions.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient process that enables simulation of Ramsey experiments and estimation of the phase is developed and used to demonstrate the Bayesian method's superiority through the modeling of experimental data. This research indicates that the Bayesian method can achieve reliable results in quantum phase measurements with higher accuracy.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. Our centrality metric, referred to as Gromov centrality, utilizes the Gromov theorem that relates the triangle inequality to shortest path lengths, enabling the measurement of centrality at multiple scales. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our multi-scale centrality in capturing network properties and predicting properties at scales greater than network size. Additionally, we translate our metric into classical centrality measures, reveal its properties and non-intuitive behaviors, and apply it to analyze and critique current measures.

From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r from the gravitational center and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Einstein's theory, including the absence of anomalous orbital accelerations and a radial energy distribution matching Newton's vacuum energy, thus precluding the existence of dark matter. This solution yields a lens equation compatible with the observed magnitude of the gravitational shift of the Mercury's orbit, and also enables the calculation of a two-body interaction force differing from Einstein's relativistic force by a factor that may be confirmed or rejected through planetary missions.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing particular characteristics, such as matching ranks among all components, can be grouped into subcategories called bundles. We establish a method for accurately calculating dimensions of these groups in the context of matrices with specific properties or zeros in specific locations, effectively addressing a initially solved but partially incorrect problem from a prior study. Additionally, our approach allows us to categorize subsets of matrices with certain zero patterns, leading to several key outcomes.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is adapted and extended to describe T-duality for twisted tori comprised of torus bundles with twisted geometric characteristics. Building upon the work of Abou-Zaid et al., who established topological T-duality for compact resolved conifolds, this framework is formulated in a geometric manner similar to physical theories. Key considerations involve defining a suitable coordinate system that accounts for global and gauged coordinates, as well as self-consistency principles governing these coordinates and their extension. This research provides practical applications by creating algebraic representations for torsion-free twisted tori and offering a step-by-step demonstration of T-duality for a simple zero-background field configuration. Consequently, the paper provides contributing evidence towards resolving a long-standing challenge in non-commutative C*-algebra formalism: defining a universal algebraic representation from a given continuous map.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le created a stochastic graph embedding method in their FOCS '20 work that allowed minor-free graphs with diameter $D$ to be embedded into graphs with treewidth $O_{\epsilon}(\log n)$ with expected distortion $+\epsilon D$. The researchers later employed this method in their STOC '21 work to create a QPTAS for minor-free graphs. Filtser and Le developed a QPTAS for minor-free graphs with Baker's metric using a different approach in their STOC '21 work. The current research develops a new embedding method that reduces the treewidth to $O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)^2$. As a result, the capacitated vehicle routing problem is resolved efficiently using a PTAS for minor-free graphs. The QPTAS running time for Baker's metric problem is improved to $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)}$. The new embedding method can also be applied to planar graphs with treewidth $O((\log\log n)^{5/3}\log n)$. The current work relies on an analysis of a new static graph embedding method that uses Lovász's local choice algorithm. An $O(\log\log n)$-approximation ratio is achieved by simulating this algorithm. The research provides an exact running time for a related problem. For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values.

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices as a controlled laboratory for understanding quantum phase transitions through eigenstate computation is compelling, even if actual calculations might be impractical without further advancements in precision. Variational quantum eigensolver approaches have shown promise, despite being susceptible to errors which can destructively affect its algorithmic process. Researchers have created a novel adaptive variational quantum eigensolver variant, utilizing the adaptive variational quantum eigensolver's ability to enhance convergence while limiting error impact on final results. By integrating a principle that applies unitary transformations to excited states without altering target wave functions, this modified adaptive variational quantum eigensolver variant achieves improved robustness and effectively mitigates noise-induced corruption, demonstrating superior outcome over the conventional adaptive variational quantum eigensolver method. Using the heuristic framework, researchers simulated computational simulations that mimicked quantum systems modeled after the one-dimensional Heisenberg model, which exhibits quantum critical behavior. Researchers found that their variant performed better than the conventional variant, yielding highly accurate outcomes, even under severe error conditions. Researchers discovered that their variant's efficacy was partly due to reduced dynamic variance at low excitation levels and pinpointed the crucial low-excitation criterion that yields such stability. Researchers specified the necessary low-excitation criterion needed and specified bounds. Researchers simulated computational simulations that mimicked quantum systems modeled after the one-dimensional Heisenberg model to determine these bounds. A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping, with techniques like variational autoencoders (VAEs) commonly used for learning such structures. Although widely applied, there are concerns regarding biased representations due to maximum likelihood estimation, as well as uncertainty in the mapping caused by combining the prior and encoder uncertainties. A new model, the deep generative decoder (DGD), is introduced to separate the mapping and prior, using a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of representations instead. This involves formulating the posterior as a product of the prior and encoder mapping. A new model, the deep generative detector (DGDd), is also proposed, which uses the DGD and adds a Gaussian noise to the latent feature, regression, and other modifications. The DGD models perform well in various experiments including 1D, 2D and 3D latent feature reconstruction, quantitive analysis of reconstruction, regularization, and the impact of the prior on the posterior, as well as in equalization and detection tasks.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be influenced by inflationary relativistic amplification of cosmic gravitational waves. This phenomenon, where the curvature perturbations evolve into the gravitational wave spectrum, may have previously been underestimated due to the properties of the background cosmological fluid. Utilizing the critical-index stochastic inflationary model, which offers quantitative and precise results regarding the potential amplification, it is shown that the required conditions could lead to a significant, observable stochastic gravitational wave signal within its frequency range of 2 - 30 nHz. Such a signal would be detectable by a potential NANOGrav follow-up experiment and future Advanced LIGO-Virgo observations. Moreover, the amplification could potentially resolve the Hubble-tension discrepancy by modifying the cosmic perturbations' equation of state, aligning with Planck data constraints.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We utilized standalone observations with the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) of the comet C/2015 ER61, conducted shortly after its significant April outburst in 2017. This enabled us to acquire unique, high-resolution interferometric data of key volatile molecules, including CS, HCN, CH3OH, H2CS, and H2CO, which were also checked against non-thermal radio emission shapes characteristic of comets. We discovered that CS, a carbon-based molecule with carbon as its source, exhibits complex behavior linked with atmospheric atmospheric ice sublimation in comet polar regions, as well as possible gas source locations within the comet nucleus itself. Our findings also validate distribution models of molecular emissions observed previously with other comets using smaller instruments. This supports models suggesting that molecular emissions observed in cometary atmospheres originate from icy cometary nuclei.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and neural text-to-speech, requiring only access to a large amount of unlabeled speech data. Our method starts by identifying distinct speakers within the data and then uses speaker-specific acoustic features to create a universal speech system. A novel technique allows for the development of a speech synthesis model without the need for labeled data, simply by manipulating the speaker information to match a random sentence. When evaluated, our system demonstrates a significant improvement in quality and divergence from standard TTS models, with a newly trained model demonstrating a 49.2% higher F1 score and 60.1% higher D1 score compared to a pre-trained model of the same architecture.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within a FRW universe. Subsequently, we develop a 
quintessence approach by introducing a dynamic potential derived from the 
stability criterion of the model under a complex form, examining both scenarios.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming (MO-MINLP) issues where each variable can be classified as integer or continuous have gained significant researchers' interest in recent years. MO-MINLP problems involve diverse applications across various disciplines such as economics, energy, chemistry, and computer networks among others. In fact, a non-linear objective function and constraint, along with multiple objectives, distinguish MO-MINLP in comparison to traditional mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) with a single objective. In solving MO-MINLP, evolutionary algorithms such as NSGAII have shown great potential in comparison to other multi-objective optimization algorithms. In order to improve computational efficiency of NSGAII, a novel algorithm known as BB-NSGAII has been proposed by integrating it with a novel branch-and-bound (BrB) strategy. In addition, BB-NSGAII has been further enhanced using enhanced computational efficiency techniques. In order to confirm the effectiveness of BB-NSGAII, comprehensive numerical experiments have been conducted on four high and low computational complexity MO-MINLP test cases with variable numbers of integer and continuous variables by varying the number of objectives from one to four. In order to confirm the validity of obtained results, BB-NSGAII has been compared with other competing algorithms such as MO-SLP, MO-APM, and NSGAII among others. We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff 1-connected Lie groupoid, when translated to internal groupoid form, is internally connected. Additionally, the internalization process preserves integral completeness.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating a purpose-built security policy language and map, as well as an administrative interface for policy management, users can conveniently authorize and revoke access during data sharing activities. Currently, Dynaswap is being utilized to support data analysis workflows within the NBAC benchmark suite and the TCGA dataset analysis.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within a piece of text. Approximately one-third of reviewed articles discuss innovative approaches for this topic, employing a distributional model to capture aspects and sentiment distributions. Unfortunately, developing such pre-trained models is complex and time-consuming, especially since incorporating supervised pre-training can simplify the process. A new method has proposed an efficient approach by leveraging supervised contrastive pre-training to learn complex distributions. Before fine-tuning this pre-trained model, it can effectively capture aspects and sentiment through a self-supervised learning framework. When put to the test on standard sentiment datasets, the results demonstrate the method's superiority over baseline models.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. We develop novel estimators for key parameters like natural effect values and absolute risk differences, which can be calculated by first determining the proportions of cases and controls in each stratum and then applying weighted estimations. We demonstrate that our methods can produce consistent results even with limited available data and show that they can be applied in both regular and weighted frameworks. We illustrate our findings using data from a study on the relationship between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and its predictors, which also includes a mediator variable, to demonstrate its applications in real-world scenarios.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for transmission limitations, while also accounting for errors due to hardware. To achieve this, both the reflective surface and transmission techniques are adjusted under the constraints of energy constraints and the variability of data being transmitted. Initially, the trade-offs between security, data transmission rate, and hardware errors due to hardware are established using the Lagrange method. Optimistic outcomes for these trade-offs are then found by simplifying the problem, initially solving the variables of the reflective surface and then the transmission techniques. Finally, the best outcomes in terms of security are found through a binary search algorithm. Simulation results show that these adjustments of the reflective surface and transmission techniques significantly boost the security of data transmission and overall data transmission rate when compared to not accounting for these effects due to hardware.

We begin by defining a value-behavior alliance for decision-making, which we later expand into a learning framework that facilitates the development of an advanced, adaptive mechanism for resampling and relabeling. This mechanism, driven by the alliance, underpins the creation of sophisticated, multi-modal perception systems, enabling data-driven, post-hoc evaluation of strategies. To establish this association, we draw on dual coding theory and the principles of hierarchical reasoning and constraint satisfaction.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings from the probe's SOAP-SCA instrument, which took 1331-millisecond time-steps over the full 12-day periods. We also used data from the probe's vector magnetometer to calculate the magnetic field's strength and direction, and we based our solar wind speed and density estimates on predictions from the open-flux method, and then applied those values in our energy flux calculations. We discovered that there was a link between an area of high magnetic field, decreased solar wind speed, and decreased radial distance to the sun in the data we collected, and we observed two types of solar wind energy patterns, one of which was characterized by low values near the sun and the other of which was associated with energy peaks near specific frequencies, around 0.4 and 1.2 megahertz in the S-wave, and we could not yet fully explain the origin of these patterns in the data we collected. These findings highlight the significance of using multiple techniques to forecast solar wind characteristics and the value of close approaches to the sun in the solar wind's acceleration process.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra as a noncommutative analog to the total space of a numerable principal bundle. By building upon the Pedersen ideal's multipliers, we transcend Gelfand-Naimark duality to create this framework. Additionally, when considering compact Hausdorff groups acting on unital C*-algebras, the finiteness of local-triviality dimension implies our proposed definition, while the G-action on A is demonstrated to possess a certain type of freeness, which is a necessary and sufficient condition for the total space to be locally trivial, especially when considering the case where the base X is homeomorphic to a compact space. This results in our proposed definition being equivalent to a fiber bundle with a specific type of noncommutative characteristic when the base X is topologically identical to a compact space.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least cardinality of a set that can act as a ultrfilter, which implies $w_1=\kappa$ and $2^{\kappa}=\kappa^{<\kappa}}$. Furthermore, we define a certain club set known as $\mathcal{A}$ that, when used in an equation $|{\mathcal{A}}\backslash A|/|\mathbb{N}|= \frac{p}{q}$, determines the existence of a specific set $A$ such that it contains an infinite number of disjoint sets and a certain ratio of its elements' sizes to $\mathbb{N}$'s matches the given fraction $p/q$. By applying an equation involving the use of $\mathcal{A}$ and a specific sequence of natural numbers known as $\{d_n\}$ that also equals $\frac{p}{q}$, it follows that $\mathcal{A}$ can be utilized to generate a sequence of disjoint sets whose indices form a club set. The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the dynamics of annihilation and creation operators within a cavity, which is treated as a $q$-deformed massless Dirac field interacting with a bosonic field. Moreover, it appears that both sub- and super-Lorentzian light speeds can arise from the coupling of these operators, leading to the prediction of enhanced and transparent regimes. Specifically, it is found that the transmission coefficient may reach 100% and the group velocity can drop to zero at distinct phases resulting from the $q$-deformation.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict both spatial and temporal changes. Without incorporating any limiters or artificial dissipation, the method preserves the hyperbolicity of the PDEs and introduces a small amount of numerical diffusion for simplification. It's proven that as long as the trained network meets certain conditions, the solution will converge to the actual solution under suitable activation and data training. This method is validated through experiments involving advection equations, shallow water equations, Allen-Cahn equations, and the biharmonic heat equation.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to establish the ALICE Collaboration's objectives for LHC Run 3 and beyond. In the upcoming LS3 shutdown, two major upgrades are scheduled, with LS3 itself featuring the replacement of the ALICE trigger system with a fully digital, high-level trigger scheme incorporating high-energy physics analysis algorithms. Targeted particle types for triggering will be confined to $p_{\rm T}$ of 0.5-5 GeV/$c$ for charged hadrons and 1-15 GeV/$c$ for muons. In parallel, LS3 involves the exchange of the ALICE experiment's two large-time projection chambers with two smaller, more advanced detectors called the Light-weight Large area Tracking Detectors. These new detectors will cover a similar scope to the original TPCs and utilize state-of-the-art micromegas technology. In addition to these changes, a future heavy-ion program at the LHC holds promise of achieving $q_{\rm PV}$ values exceeding 6. In conjunction, LS34 involves incorporating a magnet equipped with an airtight, superconducting coil filled with liquid helium vapor. Our analysis reveals that the Berry phase resulting from the entangled light cones in anti-de Sitter space can be used to detect the timelike Unruh effect that occurs when global and local time coordinates become disconnected. This disconnectivity is a hallmark of the Unruh effect and gives rise to a global phase shift representing the difference between the local temperature and the universal causal horizon temperature. We've shown that the phase shift resulting from the entanglement of light cones is proportional to the hbar/c^2 value, indicating that the Unruh effect causes a quantum system to experience a phase shift regardless of its size, contradicting previous notions that only quantum systems smaller than the causal horizon can exhibit the Unruh effect.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed annotation for over 50,000 event occurrences in eight diverse languages. This dataset exhibits high consistency across annotators and exhibits a level of complexity similar to that of existing datasets. We have also conducted a thorough analysis of this dataset and presented the results of several extraction and classification models applied to various language pairs, highlighting the efficiency of transformer-based models like BERT and XLM in multilingual settings, often surpassing monolingual models combined in ensemble settings.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for all positive line bundles with holomorphic subbundles, thus generalizing and extending previous results established by Schmid, Schaffner, and Karthik.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed an increase in hard X-ray luminosity over time for the high-mass X-ray binary Cyg X-1 when the source was in a state of intense emission. This enhancement cannot be fully explained by standard accretion disk theory. A significant factor appears to be the increased scattering of X-rays by the fast stellar wind as it approaches the disk from farther distances, following its typical trajectory. Although the wind's density at large distances is typically low, it makes a significant contribution to the overall X-ray emission in the energy range between 3-10 keV. A model that incorporates an irradiated wind that adjusts its density and temperature in response to the increasing X-ray flux, while also considering changes in the accretion disk's inner boundary and correlation effects, provides a satisfactory fit to the data. A notable outcome of this fit is that an enhancement of only 10% to 30% in the wind's density is sufficient to account for the observed evolution of the source. This result has implications for the interpretation of future observations of similar high-mass X-ray binaries with the NuSTAR and Athena space telescopes, as it suggests that the wind's scattering likely plays an essential role in shaping the source's spectrum in the energy range between 3-10 keV during the intense emission phase.

The $\mathbf G$-gauge group's non-abelian aether-like term can be written as a specific divergence based on the composite operator $\mathbf G \times \mathbf G$. By utilizing the zeta function regularization method, it's possible to determine the UV behavior of this term and confirm that it contributes to the $\Lambda^{2n}$ term in the effective action for even values of $n \geq 2$. Additionally, when temperature is factored in, the term involving $\Lambda^{2n}$ remains, along with an oscillatory term related to the MSIR function. When the temperature is set to zero, the oscillatory component disappears, leaving only the term with $\Lambda^{2n}$. A similar pattern is observed for the casimir energy of a confined Yang-Mills field, which also results in the $\Lambda^{2n}$ term contributing to the energy. For $n=2$, this energy is also present in the vacuum of the gauge field, resulting in its UV finite value directly proportional to the square of the $\bar \theta$ parameter.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two. To address this issue, we examine multiple model designs capable of tapping into rich data in the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset, parsing it alongside Universal Dependencies for a more in-depth analysis. Although the dependency parsing component benefits from the joint model, our results are hindered by inconsistencies in the syntactic annotations of the UD dataset and limitations in the semantic representations of the UDS dataset, highlighting the need for improved reference datasets for meaningful comparisons between syntax and semantics.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potentially significant event, capable of launching outflows that explain the phenomenon of short gamma ray bursts and kilonovae radiation. By utilizing the detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and Virgo and subsequently analyzing electromagnetic counterparts, we can model the central engine responsible for these events. Using the finite volume version of the general relativistic MHD code BSSN, we simulated a particular type of disk and discovered that disk instability occurs within a specified threshold in angular momentum. Following the ejection of jets from the spinning black hole, we simulated postmerger outflows using a one-dimensional approach, taking into account electron-photon interactions. Our calculations show that these outflows may exhibit speeds ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of km/s within the initial hours following the merger, influenced by various initial conditions. These outflows could lead to the radiation of radio and neutrino light with lifetimes of several days, potentially explaining fast, persistent, and radio-emitting radiation observed in GRB 211211A, however our models predict a longer duration and greater luminosity than observed in GRB 211211A's neutrino emission, with GRB 211211A's neutrino emission being below predicted limits. We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations suggested approximately 49,000 such galaxies exist on the galaxy cluster/macroscale over an 110,000,000,000,000 times larger volume, leading to an estimated merger rate of approximately 12 per 10^7 galaxies per century, specifically type-giant-giant mergers that significantly affect neighbor galaxies. Our research revealed nearly 60 percent of these mergers involve non-interacting, close-distance combinations and just under 26 percent occur within viewable star-forming interactions, with the remainder falling into a category we term 'deadly mergers,' characterized by very slowly accumulating mass, due to significant mass loss during the merger (24+/-7%). Additionally, we undertook a'modified mass-growing-modes' categorization, discovering that only one in five tidal features fall into the star-forming interaction class (23 +/-7%) and the majority occur in interactions where one galaxy dominates (~82%, +/-7%), with the rest falling into the category of equal mass interactions (~5%, +/-1%).
