This paper provides a detailed explanation of various phenomena resulting from the repulsive nature of gravity due to rotating objects and their effect on surrounding space. It identifies bipolar outflows as a consequence of this effect and proposes that many other astronomical events, such as those producing fast ejections like SN1987A's, proto-stellar jets, and the radio sources G109.5-1.0 and G43.6-0.3, are also the result of repulsive gravity caused by rapidly rotating, extremely dense objects.

We have gathered a vast data set of observations from 18 specific FRBs, consisting of simultaneous and delayed optical observations, in an effort to identify their optical counterparts and understand their behavior. This data set includes 268 registration attempts with a time difference of less than 10 days between radio and optical observations, along with 391 registration attempts with a larger time difference. Despite these efforts, we have not been able to confirm the optical counterparts of FRBs, although our research does set limits on the flux and flux density of potential counterparts. Moreover, we have analyzed the potential luminosity and spectral energy distribution of optical counterparts, including their proton antineutrino and neutrino emission, taking into account FRB 180924's persistent radio emission. While FRB 180924's luminosity may be as low as $10^{30-32}$ erg s$^{-1}$, its proposed luminosity is $10^{24-25}$ erg s$^{-1}$, a result consistent with Mpc distance and neutrino emission. To achieve a thorough understanding of FRB's optical behavior, we plan to collect even more data by observing FRB repeats and flares.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has become the standard approach for achieving high-power laser generation, with associated systems now being employed across various disciplines including optics, astronomy, biology, and national security. Nevertheless, the intricate interaction between traditional computational methods and experimental factors like heat dissipation, mechanical stability, and acoustic properties remains largely unstudied. Our research introduces a unified framework integrating these aspects to streamline the design, modeling, and reverse engineering of laser systems. This framework enables researchers to accurately predict and refine experimental settings, allowing for the efficient design of newer generation laser systems. Our methodology was put to the test in modeling the Janus II laser system at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, yielding results remarkably close to those obtained through experimental measurements.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by non-text modalities like images. We introduce a new framework called MAGIC that allows these models to perform tasks such as image captioning in the absence of explicit training data. By combining an existing language model like GPT-2 with an image-text matching model like CLIP, MAGIC provides a plug-and-play solution that guides the model's output during generation. Our research demonstrates the potential of large language models in multimodal applications, and we provide theoretical evidence of their capability using conceptual ideas such as existence proofs. We conduct extensive testing across various sub-tasks including image captioning, cold-start captioning, and concept generation, and our results show that MAGIC is competitive with current state-of-the-art models, delivering superior visual coherence and quality in its output without requiring any additional training.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype on the Nano wallet using the Nano cryptocurrency, are presented at the International Conference on Applied Mathematics and Signal Processing in 2021.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse neural networks trained on existing data can contribute to future models. This paper outlines guidelines for cooperative modeling: 1) defining objectives 2) leveraging existing data 3) structuring models 4) evaluating outcomes and 5) disseminating knowledge. Our proposed approach facilitates the integration of various machine learning methods to address pressing issues in mechanics, such as quantifying uncertainties in predictive chemistry, simulating complex fluid dynamics and elastodynamics, predicting multi-scale solid mechanics and geological flow properties, and modeling Earth's structure and dynamic behavior. The paper also discusses challenges and forecasts imminent advancements in cooperative modeling.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, investigating whether the abundance
of these mesons can be explained by a loop mechanism. Initially, the study maps the
range of four-body decay mechanisms driven by $J^{PC}=0^{(-)}$ states, then
calculates the decay width for $J^{PC}=1^{(-)}$ states. It appears that the
$\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)(\Upsilon(2S),\Upsilon(3S))\pi^+\pi^-)$
decay pathways are notably larger than those for $(10650)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-)$
and that the abundance of the four-body decay, particularly $\Upsilon(10753)\to
\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-)$, significantly surpasses that of $(10650)\to
\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-)$. Moreover, two-Meson resonance contributions, particularly
$\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S) (\Upsilon(2S),\Upsilon(3S))\pi^+\pi^-)$, exhibit
increased magnitude relative to $(10650)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-)

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach designed to solve each optimization subproblem. Unlike conventional algorithms, AskewSGD circumvents computationally intensive projections or full feasible set optimizations and enables infeasible intermediate results. AskewSGD's numerical efficiency is comparable to contemporary methods such as the straight-through gradient estimator in BinaryConnect, as well as state-of-the-art approaches like ProxQuant and LUQ. Our convergence analysis validates the robustness of AskewSGD under general objective function assumptions, while experiments confirm its effectiveness on traditional benchmarks, demonstrating performance comparable to or surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be adopting a control theorist's perspective, discussing the intricacies of modeling and their impact on the design of the most advanced robotic systems currently developed. Key topics that will be explored include the various methodologies for creating mathematical models that account for robotic structure, the types of control strategies suitable for these robots, the difficulties encountered in the modeling process, and how those challenges affect the design and properties of the robots themselves.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ - specifically its semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with $H_1$ - cannot be broken down into real unitary representations. A new method for the convolution of homogeneous series on $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ is developed, and an explicit model for the space of harmonic distributions on $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ is constructed. Moreover, our approach also provides an expansion of Harish-Chandra's theorem to the Jacobi group, as well as a characterization of the Jacobi group's unitary irreducible representations and its character formula.

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating an approach
that understands language and searches data effectively. Current neural methods
often combine text and tables but struggle due to their limited ability to
handle complex data. Conversely, decomposition-based models can break down the
verification task into manageable components, avoiding common pitfalls. Despite
their potential, few have attempted to apply decomposition to fact verification.
Our research introduces TabVeri, a novel decomposition-based model capable of
extracting key information from text and efficiently searching tables. TabVeri's
performance surpasses existing models in fact verification, achieving top-ranked
results on the WikiTables dataset. This work not only contributes a powerful
technique for verifying facts but also serves as a stepping stone for interpreting
complex datasets comprising text and tables.

The state-of-the-art in deep generative modeling involves architectures like GANs and VAEs. Yet, the limitations of these techniques, including their capacity issues and difficult training procedures, have not fully addressed the essence of generative methods, which is to flexibly manipulate data creation criteria. Our work demonstrates a simple, effective way to incorporate prior knowledge into these generative models. By applying factor analysis, this method represents data in a lower-dimensional space while preserving their original distribution. Our approach can be universally applied to both GAN and VAE techniques.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used that selects prior samples satisfying the likelihood threshold. Researchers have developed various methods to achieve this, many of which involve discrete sampling steps. A recent study introduces and evaluates a new method, signaling, in the context of flat and log-flat priors. The research compared this method to existing approaches, including the simplified nested sampling algorithm and an improved version of its original form. The signaling method was applied to log-flat priors using a dynamic memory scheme that adapts to sampling progress. Results from 21 tests indicate the signaling method outperforms the SNES and its improved variant in terms of computation efficiency, a finding that prompted the development of a Python implementation and the conduct of additional comparisons with flat priors. Further analysis of the signaling method revealed its suitability for its original purpose, as well as potential uses in its modified form. A new Python implementation, PySign, was developed to this end, along with recommendations for future enhancements. Compared to SNES, PySign requires fewer CPU operations. Analysis demonstrates that signaling method can take advantage of flat prior properties. It outperforms SNES on the critical SNI challenge. PySign performs better than SNES in all tests. It uses fewer operations than SNES. It uses static memory, not affecting its general approach. A detailed explanation is provided in the sign sampler documentation. It has been incorporated into the nested sampling Python library ASTROPY. A general release is

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with adding weight to the edges of a graph, ensuring that the total weight of any path between two vertices of at least k+1 length is always valid. We develop a random approach to construct this, which works in any scenario with a given probability greater than 3/5. We demonstrate this by labelling a random 3-colorled planar graph with n vertices in O(n) time and expected storage of O(n/(k-1)), after which we can answer distance queries in O(log k) time. This result aligns with the current best storage efficiency achieved in fault-tolerant shortest paths, which was designed for the uniform random planar graph model. Furthermore, in contrast to existing research, our method is versatile and applicable to a wide range of graphs, including those with a given probability of at least 3/5. We extend the random 3-color d-vertex joining model, developed by Bernstein et al., which is used to analyze the random 4-color planar graph model, used to analyze the performance of Bernstein et al., by introducing a new d-value for storage efficiency. We confirm that our model is versatile by proving that for k=2, approximately k*(k/3+1)*n vertices are needed, which is very close to the current best storage efficiency achieved in fault-tolerant shortest paths, which was designed for the uniform random planar graph model.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that decline when the model's imaginary Liouvillian gap becomes smaller, a behavior reminiscent of Bose condensation oscillations. When the model reaches a steady state just beyond the phase transition, we demonstrate that by analyzing frequency spectra of the same correlation function, we can identify distinct components, including one corresponding to critical behavior and the other resembling Bose condensation. We cross-check these findings by analyzing two alternative correlation functions, one based on time and the other on frequency domains.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There is a common misconception that deep neural networks excel at identifying out-of-distribution samples, but such claims are largely based on training models on data from a specific distribution and then testing them on data with different characteristics. However, in medical imaging, it is often desirable to integrate data from various sources, which may have distinct distributions. As a result, a deeper understanding of how to effectively identify out-of-distribution samples is needed. This work presents an approach that combines two Gaussian process layers with an uncertainty-based metric for detection. When applied to a realistic medical imaging scenario, it becomes evident that a straightforward classification model fails to identify out-of-distribution samples, whereas the proposed approach successfully detects such samples with both higher accuracy and robustness.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat gain due to resonant excitations, typically leading to random energy distribution among various eigenstates. In contrast, a system consisting of a one-dimensional optical lattice, driven by a monochromatic light and coupled to a bath with two-level emitters, exhibits a unique thermodynamic behavior. Here, heat-induced phase transitions occur in a specific two-mode scenario where one mode remains delocalized and the other exhibits minima-like localised behaviour. Through numerical investigations it is demonstrated that this two-mode system exhibits a range of non-equilibrium thermodynamic behaviors including phase transitions, critical behaviors and pseudo-gap phenomena. These findings provide valuable insights into both understanding heat-induced phase transitions in intricate many-body systems and exploring heat-induced transitions in isolated systems through the use of a proxy model of interacting quantum systems at finite temperatures.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding relates Alexandrov's maximum principle for convex functions, and this result has significant implications for the $\alpha$-H\"older continuity of the solution for a given value of $\alpha$ in the interval $(0,1]$.

Counting methods that are both precise and reliable in timescales of minutes are scarce. We've developed an analytical framework to identify time-domain patterns in incoherent counting signals with wide timing ranges. This framework helps filter out noise and pinpoint a logical system's operation point. With this information, one can determine the minimum recording duration needed for accurate time-domain analysis of an optical clock system. Our approach was successfully applied to two incoherent counting systems, yielding accurate phase information for two logical operators in both systems.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) control planes to address network failures in fog-computed networks (FCN). The proposal involves implementing a distributed control plane in the fog layer to manage the lifecycle of service models (SMs) in Service Function Chains (SFCs). The approach includes three strategies: fault prevention, fault detection, and fault response. The first strategy involves utilizing K-means clustering and control logic distribution to prevent faults based on time-sensitive data. The second strategy employs real-time detection methods using clustering and control logic sharing. The proposed response strategy in the fog layer enables resource management and failure recovery in SFCs through recalculation of service models and efficient resource allocation, which is both energy-efficient and complies with quality of service (QoS) requirements. The proposed concept was validated through experimentation and offers improvements in energy efficiency and network resource usage.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the position of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables us to develop a method for determining which loss functions are compatible and can be combined. This new approach, 'gradient surgery,' allows us to devise a highly effective, streamlined learning procedure. When applied to a pre-trained model, the result is consistent, high performance results in multiple benchmark tests.

In this context, we explore error correction codes based on holographic principles and self-correcting mechanisms that apply to quantum systems, which can be simulated using tensor networks, particularly the holographic, PEPS-based Maurer-Ryu code. This code has a 'physical' nature similar to that of holographic error correction codes found in gravitational theories. The self-correcting properties of the code rely on a special column that regulates the interaction between local modifications and noise and a 'plausible' Eraser operation, which remains computationally tractable. The self-correcting mechanism introduces a hierarchy of renormalization scales, which enhances the computational complexity of the code. The code's ability to correct errors with high accuracy is achieved through a process called hyper-contracting, which combines multiple scales of renormalization, resulting in an invariant manifold resistant to local alterations. The code's eigenvalues, volume law scaling, and spectral gap properties are investigated, which influence its ability to correct and tolerate faults. The properties demonstrate a 'plausible' connection to the stability conditions of holographic error correction codes, with some signals of strict mathematical relationships. The code's stability enables the realization of computationally intensive tasks without precision loss, such as calculating entanglement entropy across the boundary, which involves a two-dimensional lattice with interactions and has high computational requirements. The code's approximations, computational costs, and potential completeness are also investigated, which involves a contractive renormalization process simulating the holographic

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes MeerKAT data by examining the distances between groups of these filaments. A sample of 43 groupings containing 174 radio filaments was studied and their shapes were analyzed. Many grouped filaments were found to resemble harp strings or comets with looped tails, in contrast to the mostly straight filaments that lie perpendicular to the galactic plane. We also observed filaments that split into two at a single point, which may be due to the movement of plasma through the filaments. Changes in the spectral index, brightness and curvature of the filaments along their length do not follow a regular pattern. Distances between filaments within groups range from 0.04 to 0.65 pc and show no correlation with other properties. A hierarchical clustering and robust estimation algorithm was used to determine the average distance between filaments in groups: 0.29 pc. This average distance correlates with estimated filament widths, suggesting that they are not randomly formed. A simulation of random distances yielded a significantly lower average, indicating that the actual structure of the filaments plays a role in their spacing. A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs and load response through the use of PRI#V, a primary-secondary coupled voltage control strategy. The method utilizes a primary control layer to adjust power injection and a secondary control layer to adjust phase angles of node voltages. Fierro et al.'s formulation is built upon to develop two decentralized algorithms - an optimal linear control algorithm in MatLab and a more practical, yet sub-optimal algorithm in C, aiming for minimal computing time and usability in real-world systems. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparison with two existing approaches on both simulated and real-world datasets.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have received considerable attention, considering arm-dependent delays adds an increased level of difficulty, even for the simple experts problem. In the case where delays are consistently consistent above a certain threshold, we develop a strategy resulting in a 190.3 factor improvement over the best-known algorithms for experts; this outcome is nearly optimal, given we establish a lower bound indicating at least 190.3 factors. When arm-dependent delays are intrinsic, we succeed in developing improved algorithms for both experts and bandits, achieving performance within a factor of 5 of the optimal, a threshold we establish is approaching perfectly with increased precision.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model training. A novel theoretical framework has been developed for generating text in dialogue, surpassing existing theories by allowing analysis of multiple goals inherent to text-generation. The new framework also provides theoretical guarantees for learners that adapt to unseen data. By applying this model, researchers can pinpoint a task-oriented dialogue system's underlying objective, identify a suitable reward function, and understand the impact of sequence-length on learning performance. The theoretical framework also enabled the derivation of the first task-independent bounds on the sample complexity of task-oriented dialogue systems. The suggested changes to the reward function and the training data result in significant improvements in lexical diversity while maintaining task success for a benchmark dataset.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from over four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled.

A technique for predicting the stress of turbine components in offshore windfarms, based on physical modeling, is developed and improved. By applying statistical analysis to data from model tests, a predictive model is created that can accurately simulate the probability of excessive stress and the associated probability of failure. To increase efficiency, this model integrates fast computational models, known as surrogates, which in this case is a Gaussian process regression. By combining multiple levels of predictive models, our approach, known as chained Gaussian process, enables the calculation of stress loads with high precision, while requiring only a few computational steps. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations of model tests, resulting in a significant reduction of computational cost, from 1/600 to 1/120 compared to previous methods.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis management and policy development. This research focuses on utilizing Twitter analytics to gauge the initial reactions of people towards the 2020 Izmir earthquake, considering the timely reporting and widespread reach of this social platform. By combining data analytics and machine learning methodologies, our study reveals the demographic characteristics of Twitter users who shared their thoughts about the earthquake and its associated symptoms, providing valuable insights for crisis managers to assess public emotions and perceptions during catastrophic events. The findings of this research can serve as a benchmark for future studies examining public reactions on social media during crises.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we establish the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of the Solvable Baumslag-Solitar group BS(1,n), which verifies a conjecture of Khan.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules in different environments. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements and structural changes. Furthermore, this new approach is shown to be more efficient and effective than other data analysis methods, particularly in experiments involving a large number of data points and where the reliability of some experimental data is uncertain.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with realistic driving scenarios encompassing diverse
trajectories and driving behaviors. SceNDD features a comprehensive set of data,
including the ego-vehicle's trajectory, velocity, and yaw angle, as well as
third-person views along with lane and acceleration information. Our method
yields over 7,800 unique scenarios. We showcase the utility of SceNDD by using
it to train and evaluate a sum-product automaton model responsible for
predicting the movements of other vehicles. Several existing datasets, such as
NDD and NuScenes, are outperformed by SceNDD in terms of both real-world scenario
reproduction and longer-term forecasting. Our create-a-create approach enables
the production of more accurate and naturalistic datasets. SceNDD is made publicly
available on GitHub.

In the context of Conformal Field Theory, reflected entropy has been explored as a measure of the minimal entanglement between a pair of regions, with key applications in interface/boundary CFT. Various insights have been established through holographic constraints; for instance, its connection to the minimal entanglement entropy and a temperature-dependent component proportional to the central charge. A subsequent analysis using the conformal collapse method revealed that reflected entropy grows no faster than a quadratic rate with temperature in one-dimensional systems. Building upon this, our approach develops a general reflection symmetry framework for one-dimensional systems and, as a result, establishes that reflected entropy is mirrored in its dependence for the two-dimensional cross-channel and central charge components. This new understanding enables us to further prove that reflected entropy grows no faster than a quadratic rate with temperature in two-dimensional spacetimes. These findings align with predictions from the holographic reflection symmetry perspective.

Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference effectively. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized cyclic prefix resulting from additional cascaded RIS channels, as well as nonlinear distortions stemming from hardware imperfections. To tackle these challenges, an advanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based channel estimation method (eELM-BC) is introduced in this research to ensure accurate channel estimation. Building upon a model-driven framework, least square (LS) estimation is applied initially to highlight the linear features necessary for channel estimation. Following this step, an integrated ELM network is created based on the identified LS features, enabling the formulation of a linear regression matrix for channel estimation. Finally, a zero-order additive correction technique is combined with the proposed method to rectify nonlinear distortions. Our simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed eELM-BC method outperforms existing methods in terms of various performance metrics.

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being observed with unsharp, non-projective measurement methods. We establish work by comparing pre and post-measurement state energy differences both before and after multiple conditional measurements. We demonstrate that, for a specific type of unsharp measurement, the work expression reduces to the projective measurement case even in the presence of multiple measurements. If the measurement is strong enough, it will always satisfy an equality which we refer to as the integral fluctuation theorem. Our analysis generalizes previous findings and we are also able to broaden the applicability of Rexact work by considering multiple, unsharp measurements. As a related application, we examine the conditions under which work fluctuation values will be non-negative when performing projective measurements. We find that this condition is satisfied if the effective Hamiltonian of the observed system is Hermitian. Our results will be verified via numerical simulations.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Clifford algebras. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the space of self-commutators of the instanton's associated Dirac operator. For nearly parallel G2-manifolds with non-compact tangent directions, this deformation space can be represented as a finite-dimensional vector space. We provide specific examples related to an S1-bundle over CP2, each featuring a vanishing first Chern class and an instanton of second type.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has posed an unprecedented challenge to public healthcare systems, prompting a wide array of innovative technological interventions to combat the disease. In numerous countries, the implementation of contact tracing COVID-19 apps has emerged as a primary strategy for managing the virus's progression and protecting the safety of individuals in the community. As these contact tracing apps gather sensitive user data, raising concerns about user privacy, this study seeks to investigate the measures being taken to safeguard user privacy in the context of contact tracing COVID-19 apps, particularly in Brazil, where the 'Coronav\'irus-SUS' app has been adopted. This app, which relies on Bluetooth Low Energy technology to identify potential infections, allows users to voluntarily submit their data to the public healthcare system for analysis and risk assessment. By designing a conceptual framework based on the fundamental principles of data protection, this study seeks to evaluate the compliance of the Coronav\'irus-SUS app with these principles and determine the steps required for its full implementation. Furthermore, the research aims to identify key lessons that can be applied to similar apps in other countries, leading to a broader discussion on the private management of sensitive user data during public health crises.

The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in mental functions, the unique principles of quantum physics may offer a deeper, probabilistic understanding of the world. This deceptively simple yet complex phenomenon has sparked an indigo debate within the scientific community regarding the relationship between quantum physics and the human brain. In particular, some theories propose that the symptoms of neurodegenerative diseases could be treated by preserving or enhancing neural function, which is also a primary goal in areas of medicine that focus on neuroprotection and restoration. This article sets out to explore the potential of quantum physical phenomena in neural systems and the implications for both biology and medicine.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings reveal a specific four-body resonance sequence driven by combinations of Neptune's mass and orbital velocity perturbations. The multi-center coordinate system allows for a precise modeling of the resonances within the framework. The numerical results demonstrate that the resonances start influencing Iochroma slightly in its orbital history, lasting approximately 20 years. This analysis also uncovers a sixth-degree model capable of accurately explaining Iochroma's orbital behavior. Our research also explores the dynamics of the other captured objects, showing that the resonance will affect their orbital evolution in the long term.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and shares similarities with the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's identity.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Hoelzel's thesis can be expressed as the homology of a certain loop space, specifically the T-rational loop space of P(T x V), the product of the T-action space and V. This identifies the T-equivariant cohomology of P(V) as being isomorphic to the T-rational cohomology of P(T x V). Next, we demonstrate that this approach can be generalized to the calculation of rational T x Delta T-equivariant cohomology of P(V). Furthermore, our results also provide insight into the Tor-like groups relating T-rational cohomology theories through their reduction to the Tor of universal elliptic cohomology theories.

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, as well as offering a chance to use unsupervised  
methods to analyze geometrical data. A primary aspect of this project involves understanding  
how to use geometry within machine learning, as well as how artificial intelligence can be applied  
to advance mathematical research. This discussion is featured as a chapter within the book,  
Machine learning and Algebraic Geometry, edited by A. Kasprzyk.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order investigation into the angular distributions of the $J/\psi$ production $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ at an energy of approximately 10.6 GeV. Our detailed calculations include the contributions of the dominant non-relativistic QCD processes, $\Upsilon(5S) \to \eta_c,J \chi_c$ via charm annihilation, as well as the $c \bar c \to J/\psi \eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ process via one-photon and $W$-box diagrams. These computations reveal that the magnitude of the latter process significantly surpasses that of the former. Additionally, we have performed a comparative analysis of our calculated angular distributions with the experimental measurements obtained from the BESIII collaboration. Our findings demonstrate satisfactory agreement between theory and experiment.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the true purpose of PINs and the features they offer could be beneficial.

This technical note details the development of a method for precisely integrating solar profiles into energy management systems, addressing the inherent variability of solar input. A Gaussian quadrature rule has been formulated to compute the solar irradiance integrand with high accuracy, and applicable rules have been established for flux values at 10-minute intervals across the entire Earth. This quadrature rule offers efficient integration with minimal points, as evidenced by a rule requiring just 43 points to achieve an absolute error of less than 0.5 W/m^2 in Antarctica and 1.0 W/m^2 elsewhere.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in mini-batch datasets. Our new model, ViViT, capitalizes on the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation without introducing additional simplifications, enabling efficient computation of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and per-sample directional derivatives. This allows ViViT to achieve superior performance in a range of complex optimization problems and maintain scalability for large model architectures.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As a result, incorporating information about grammatical gender into representations of inanimate objects may refine our understanding of these objects, regardless of whether we're discussing living things or not. In theory, incorporating grammatical gender into these representations could bridge the gap between a word's meaning in a specific context and its broader, culturally ingrained significance, although this might also introduce unnecessary variability if two sentences with different grammatical genders possess equivalent semantic meanings. To investigate this, we conducted an analysis by comparing how well inanimate object representations, now incorporating grammatical gender, perform relative to those without in this grammatically nuanced class. Our findings show that incorporating grammatical gender improves the accuracy of these representations, indicating that incorporating this additional factor can lead to more precise interpretations of inanimate objects across different contexts.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Estimating an object's pose, a crucial aspect of visual computing, is particularly challenging when objects are categorized at a broader level rather than a more refined level.  This method, called zero-shot categorized object pose estimation, is developed to address this harder, more applied problem where there's no assumption that the object's pose can be directly learned from a set of annotated images of the same category.  This task is defined by incorporating a language model that can generate category-level object pose annotations.  This method introduces new datasets, including category-level pose annotations for the training dataset Pascal VOC.  The results from multiple datasets indicate that zero-shot categorized object pose estimation offers a promising, efficient way to obtain results, showing significant improvement over a baseline that relies on refined category-level poses.  The method's source code will be publicly available.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at 10.5281/bbdcf9f2.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, we apply VACA to assess counterfactual fairness in classification tasks, as well as train fair classifiers that maintain high performance standards.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. Although top-performing algorithms such as the Cross-correlation Pipeline for Real-time Estimation (CPRest) and the Fully Integrated Pipeline for Real-time Estimation (FIPRE) efficiently produce scientific results in fractions of a millisecond, their high-performance execution comes with a hefty price tag. This work showcases two high-performance computing implementations of the CPRest algorithm for LOFAR data, including one based on graph streams and another using CPU caches, and both of these approaches outperform traditional time-domain methods. Furthermore, we develop and release REALTA, an advanced real-time radio interferometer processing toolset that facilitates fast and accurate processing of LOFAR data. This article outlines REALTA's capabilities and highlights its substantial computational and memory efficiency gains over time-domain and graph-based methods, and demonstrates its suitability for various LOFAR data processing applications.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth and innovation in photonics and communications technology. For instance, the advancement of optical fiber-based communication systems harnessed AI's ability to balance optical considerations with electrical circuit design. Building upon this, the integration of AI-driven design of photonic devices will empower the development of large-scale, high-strength optical systems. This article will explore the initial outcomes and promising potential of metaphotonics, merging optics and electronics on a photon-based platform. Furthermore, it will examine the role AI-driven design will play in advancing metaphotonics, allowing for the cost-effective creation of massive optical systems with unparalleled performance capabilities.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become even more crucial than in recent years. Despite the numerous methods available for film revenue prediction, the most commonly used index for film evaluation - gross revenue - remains understudied. This research presents a newly created, extensive dataset of 2,916 movies comprising key attributes and the gross revenue of their home markets. A novel composite feature consisting of primary attributes was developed to provide a more comprehensive representation of film characteristics. By examining the interplay between 15 distinct features, the study reveals that a universal revenue-generating formula does not exist. However, the research identifies specific attributes or their interactions capable of significantly influencing gross revenue in varying contexts.

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
guarantees the stability of a particular system and also noting an observed 
stabilizing influence on voltage dynamics despite only analyzing secondary 
frequency control.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units of interconnected systems, known as systems of systems (SoS). This sovendoping trend in industrial networks is not well-received by network security measures, which primarily focus on individual CPS components. To rectify this, security solutions must adapt to sovendoping by ensuring the resilience of cyber and physical layers. This can be achieved by utilizing artificial intelligence-based security approaches that are aware of sovendoping, facilitating the monitoring, detection, and response to emerging sovendoping risks. Our work introduces a CPS SoS model that powers SoS with intelligence, incorporating AI to sovendoping detect sovendoping and elevate overall system resilience.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions exhibit a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to various physical phenomena. Two of these phenomena, the UV-excess and X-ray excess, are characterized by distinct power-law indices, $\alpha_{UV}$ and $\alpha_X$, respectively. Analyzing the UV-excess requires sophisticated radiative transfer codes, whereas the X-ray excess can often be approximated with a simpler power-law model. Both the UV and X-ray excess features are typically associated with a single, coherent emission mechanism in blazars. We employ a Monte-Carlo code, Monte-Carlo Non-thermal Processes (MONTANA), in conjunction with the Monte-Carlo Applications for Partially Polarized Inverse External-Compton Scattering (MAPPIES) code to model the X-ray excess. Both codes are capable of simulating complex inverse Compton scattering processes, which are often responsible for the UV-excess and potentially the UV/soft X-ray excess. We analyze a subset of 56 active galactic nuclei (AGN) with high signal-to-noise ratios and observe agreement between observational data and the MAPPIES code simulations for 29 sources. Additionally, we identify 27 sources that exhibit discordant results and discuss potential causes. To account for discrepancies, we introduce a new emission component representing thermal X-ray radiation from the accretion disk.

In our study of intricate multi-dimensional environments, also known as complex landscapes, we explored their categorization based on distinct saddle types, which proves relatively straightforward. Contrasting this is the situation involving quasi-energy landscapes, which result from intricate patterns of combinations. Here, the process of advancing to higher dimensional sub-spaces, known as analytic continuation, proves to be quite complex and requires careful navigation through various dimensional transitions. To demonstrate the progress in understanding complex landscapes, we successfully applied the technique to two models: the Voglbacher et al model and another involving biased torus.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for analyzing multiple state copies in real-time.  These optimized methods utilize specific measurements, may be adaptive and only use each copy's local properties, resulting in the potential for a more resilient process that can still produce optimal results even with partial data loss.  By highlighting existing research that shows local measurement methods are capable of achieving global optimal results with binary and specific three-state systems under specific conditions, we can identify potential challenges that could limit the global method's performance in real-time for more complex multi-state systems. Specifically, our research shows that when dealing with systems of any dimension that can be represented as a symmetric expression, local measurement methods can achieve perfect global results with a sufficient number of states. However, our research reveals that when dealing with systems of an odd dimension that can be represented as a symmetric expression and where measurement is based on a single copy's local properties, local measurement methods cannot consistently produce perfect global results with a sufficient number of states. Ultimately, our research shows that when dealing with systems of any dimension that can be represented as a symmetric expression and where measurement is based on a series of data, local measurement methods can achieve perfect global results with a sufficient number of states.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass spectrum of light mesons, can replicate the masses of light baryons.

In the field of solar physics, researchers use a technique called helioseismology to study the Sun's interior. It involves analyzing the shifts in wavelength of sunlight emitted from the Sun's atmosphere, which reveals its rotation speed. By combining data from different angles, scientists can gain a better understanding of how the Sun's atmosphere rotates. However, observations suggest that there is a discrepancy between the shift in wavelength and the Sun's rotation, which cannot be explained by the Sun's internal rotation. Several theories, such as the solar jet phenomenon, have been proposed to account for this discrepancy. In this study, scientists re-examined the impact of solar jets and other active features on the shift in wavelength. They used computer simulations of the Sun's atmosphere to model how these features might affect the Sun's rotation speed as measured by the MDI instrument. Their results indicate that while solar jets and other active features have a significant effect on local measurements, their influence becomes less pronounced when viewed from a wider perspective. Interestingly, scientists found that regions surrounding active areas, such as those surrounding a solar flare, contribute more to the discrepancy than the jets themselves. They propose that fluctuations in this surrounding region could explain a significant portion of the discrepancy between the shift in wavelength and the Sun's internal rotation. They also provide a possible explanation for these fluctuations and show that they could be responsible for the discrepancy observed in the study.

This research examines the potential gravitational waves originating from cosmic strings and early magnetic fields that can be detected within the frequency range of pulsar timing arrays. The analysis reveals that powering gravitational waves until the present day requires very little energy. For magnetic fields, this means the energy density needs to be higher than the universe's energy density at the epoch of formation, which seems plausible given the known large-scale features of our universe's magnetic field. To the contrary, achieving this requirement might be difficult for cosmic strings due to the constraints imposed by big bang nucleosynthesis. A dedicated PTA observation campaign can potentially detect the source of early magnetic fields' gravitational waves, offering insights into this phenomenon. A suitable follow-up observation approach, requiring minimal resources, is outlined.

Light field technology is currently being used in various applications due to its ability to accurately preserve 4D spatial information. A significant challenge arises during the processing of compressed light fields, as local image distortions lead to unclear object boundaries and require specialized handling. Our proposed method tackles this issue by first training a disparity model to forecast these local deviations, allowing for the effective adaptation of image compression algorithms to the specific characteristics of the given light field. In contrast to existing methods, our approach does not require controlled in-studio capture of reference images to achieve refined compression results. Our experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of the disparity model in enhancing the efficiency of compressed light fields, achieving up to an 8-fold reduction in file size with minimal deterioration in PSNR values and outperforming other top-performing image compression methods.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, we can adopt interactive models, such as supervised learning, or non-interactive approaches like retrieval-based methods. We analyze the benefits of combining these strategies in a hybrid framework and demonstrate that by pre-training with non-interactive models and fine-tuning with interactive models, we can achieve significant performance improvements, with gains of up to +3.35 mNDCG for zero-shot settings and +0.96 mNDCG for few-shot settings. This hybrid framework proves to be robust under data scarcity and is worthy of further exploration in vector-based cross-lingual IR research.

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, particularly those aimed at understanding childhood mortality rates in Kenya. For this purpose, we have developed several approaches using both administrative boundaries and spatial models to analyze data from surveys, all of which leverage a synthetic estimation technique. Our experiments reveal that a modeled-based methodology provides more accurate results, suggesting a strong association between environmental factors and mortality rates, with differences between districts often revealed through a multi-way analysis. Mortality rates are generally higher in rural areas, with variations tied to education, urbanization, and regional income levels. Our research suggests that a modeled-based methodology can be an effective choice for statistical surveys and programs, particularly those operating in developing contexts where access to various data sources may be limited.

The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing betting situations where the gambler's winnings are encoded in a quantum memory's intrinsic properties, rather than the conventional payout. We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as suggested by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and its expected value in thermal equilibrium. In this scenario, semi-classical thermal fluctuations facilitate upper limiting expectations for variable bets. We also explore the implications of a quantum memory's intrinsic non-classical features on variable bets. Furthermore, our work lays the groundwork for further research into quantum financial markets.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of monolayer compounds MA$_2$Z$_4$ involves in-depth analysis of their band structure and excitons using ab initio GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation approaches. The results obtained for all 24 variations of MoSi$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$N$_4$, TiSi$_2$N$_4$, MoGe$_2$N$_4$, WGe$_2$N$_4$, TiGe$_2$N$_4$, MoSi$_2$P$_4$, WSi$_2$P$_4$, TiSi$_2$P$_4$, MoGe$_2$P$_4$, WGe$_2$P$_4$, and TiGe$_2$P$_4$ reveal quasiparticle energy dispersion characterised by distinct bands such as flat band, van Hove features, and snail shape, which correlate with the alignment of wave functions of the conduction and valence states. Furthermore, our predictions show that a stacking-independent and anisotropic exciton, comparable to that of MoS$_2$, emerges in each of the 21 Wurtzite and three Tetragonal semiconductor structures investigated, which provides theoretical grounds for the observed exciton, offers recommendations for potential p-type single-layer semiconductors, and suggests that many-membered stacks of these compounds will

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to be pivotal in the process of stellar formation, but due to simplicity, hydrodynamical models have traditionally been the norm in protostellar disk modeling.  We investigate the initial protostellar disk development using high-resolution simulations that take into account magnetic field effects, radiative transfer, complete rotational balance, and magnetic breaking limits in the mean gas density. Our findings show that magnetic influence and non-ideal factors coordinate to create an almost flat, thin disk from the collapse of a core, resembling the solidus disk observed with ATOMS. We discovered that both magnetic field and non-ideal factors play a crucial part in disk formation, particularly in its outer regions. While magnetic field dominates, non-ideal factors are preeminent in the center of the disk. We analyzed how magnetic reconnection affects the disk's structure and found that inside the disk, particularly in the outer region, gravitational collapse happens at a slower rate due to non-ideal factors, whereas in the upper layers, gravitational collapse happens at a faster rate due to magnetic field effects. Completeness of rotational balance, magnetic breaking limits, and radiative transfer simulations yield a thin, flat solidus disk with a unique snow-line structure that reflects changing chemical compositions throughout the disk formation process.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional BTSM models are often insufficient because they fail to account for several significant factors, such as sudden spikes, periodic trends, and relationships with other time series in the data set. In response, this paper's BTSM extension with varying decay rates at each time step integrates all these key elements, while its Bayesian formulation allows for reliable statistical analysis. However, generating samples from the high-dimensional distribution of the model parameters within this framework is highly resource-intensive. As a result, this paper's primary contribution is the development of a refined Bayesian variational inference and learning strategy for the model. This strategy enables streamlined approximate posterior inference and reliable model learning through advanced variational inference techniques. Moreover, this paper's approach addresses issues related to model selection, outlier resistance, and the learning of multiple time series data. Finally, empirical evaluations of the model are conducted using a diverse collection of financial and sensor time series data.

In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by treating Pontryagin duality as a particular instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group $A$, and its associated group $\mathcal F$ of continuous homomorphisms from $A$ to the circle group $\mathbb T$, where $(A,+)$ along with $\mathcal F$ form a continuous logic structure $M. Consequently, the local type space $S_\mathcal F(M)$ directly corresponds to the Pontryagin dual of the group $\mathcal F$ if it is viewed isolatedly, and this correspondence reveals fine detail regarding the topological characteristics of $A$. Specifically, this implies that if $A$ possesses the indiscrete topology, then $S_\mathcal F(M)$ encompasses the spectrum of the unitary dual of the group $\mathcal F$.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A notable observation is the coexistence of distinct ethical considerations in various settings, necessitating a unified approach that tackles multiple concerns at once. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the challenges and proposes a unified framework for mitigating bias and safeguarding privacy in the context of federated learning-based deep learning. To achieve this goal, we thoroughly examine the underlying techniques, examine their interconnections, and outline future research avenues.

We propose a supersymmetric expansion of a basic $U(1)_X$ model with a new, TeV-scale particle that acts as dark matter and features a novel $Z'$ boson decay characteristic - 50% decays into the left-handed neutrino and right-handed partner, along with to electrons and photons. In this model, we investigate how to control neutrino masses through tribosonic neutrino coupling at the one-loop level. Additionally, we examine why this model is not in conflict with existing observational data on dark matter, as well as potential signs of its presence that could be detected at the Large Hadron Collider in the near future.

We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive pilot signal to a number of energy harvesting receivers. The surface is configured in a manner that optimizes energy reception for all receivers while also maintaining their reception signals separate, maximizing each receiver's absorbed energy. Due to the continuous nature of the reflecting surface parameters, we formulate the problem as a non-linear optimization issue and use a novel deep autoencoder-based method to find a accurate low-dimensional solution quickly and efficiently. Our results demonstrate that the proposed neural network not only accurately reproduces the original parameters but also generalizes well to similar parameters, enabling it to effectively handle uncertainty in the system by applying it to unseen energy transmitter positions. Moreover, the proposed method surpasses traditional optimization methods, notably the genetic algorithm.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of the calculated proton-neutron coupling and the residual Pauli exclusion principle forces. However, utilizing only the calculated Gamow-Teller strength resulted in higher calculated half-life values for both isotopes. Notably, this methodology can be applied more broadly to evaluate the performances of various forces beyond the Skyrme force.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the connection between right-handed neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis centers around a resonant leptogenesis mechanism that produces baryon asymmetry through TeV-level right-handed neutrino masses. A viable parameter space is established to satisfy relic density constraints, which is particularly flexible when the scalar fields' mixing is substantial. Our findings demonstrate that dark matter in this model can not only mitigate baryon asymmetry but also amplify it through the process of dark matter annihilation into pairs of right-handed neutrinos, even when dark matter is less massive than its right-handed counterpart. This amplified effect is contingent upon the dark matter and right-handed neutrino masses, $m_{\chi}$ and $m_N$ respectively, allowing for increased baryon asymmetry when $m_N$ equals 50 GeV.

We have designed a novel learning-based controller called L2R (Learn to Reach) that enables robots to achieve multiple tasks using limited experimental data and utilizes additional information about a task's dynamics. By assuming that multiple tasks share similar characteristics, L2R achieves several advantages, including reduced data requirements, improved sample efficiency, and increased experimentation options. Additionally, L2R maximizes the expected value of a task's reward function, does not require modeling task dynamics, and can simultaneously tackle an unspecified number of tasks. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of L2R in real-world scenarios such as navigating different fluids with a robot fish and establishing a framework for its future advancements, as well as developing more intensive experimentation methods.

The Toda conformal field theory based on ${\rm SL}_3/{\bf Z}_2$ with ${\rm SL}_3$ tower is used to formulate ward identities that underpin the emergent Toda hydrodynamic system. This Toda hydrodynamic system is derived from the ${\rm SL}_3$ tower's current algebra. Ward identities for both the chiral primary operators generated by the ${\rm SL}_3$ tower and the 't Hooft-like self-dual variables are formulated to describe soliton packing in the Toda lattice gap. By using these ward identities, the dynamics of multiple solitons within this gap can be explicitly calculated. As a result, the dynamics of ${\rm SL}_3$ self-dual domain wall geometries can also be explicitly determined.

Despite recent advancements in the field of Deep Learning for visual downstream tasks, generating realistic images remains an ongoing challenge. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN)-based architectures for GANs. Nevertheless, these approaches often neglect to exploit valuable inter-image relationships in the training process. In an effort to leverage such relationships, researchers introduced the Relation Network (RN), which utilizes distance measures like the Euclidean distance or Cosine similarity. In this paper, a novel RN-based GAN architecture is proposed, incorporating the triplet loss to refine image embeddings and achieve improved results. Specifically, this approach demonstrates its effectiveness on two complex image synthesis tasks: multi-image image generation and text-to-image synthesis. In-depth evaluations using high-resolution datasets, including COCO and CUB, reveal that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frames and quantum frames. Reference frames serve as a basis for establishing a universal phase reference, allowing us to achieve TF-QKD without the use of phase locking. Through data post-processing and an efficient fast Fourier transform-based algorithm, the phase reference can be reconciled efficiently. As a result, TF-QKD without phase locking is made feasible over a wide range of distances on standard optical fibers. At a distance of 50 kilometers, our system is able to achieve a secret key rate of 1.27 megabits per second. Moreover, our approach enables repeater-like scalability with a secret key rate of 34 times higher than what would be achieved by conventional means at a distance of 504 kilometers. This method presents a practical means for the secure exchange of information over long distances in real-world applications.

In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space with 1 < p < ∞.  Let BUC(ℂⁿ) and BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) represent collections of uniformly bounded and continuous functions on ℂⁿ and ℬ_ᵐ (ℂⁿ's unit ball) respectively.  On the p-Fock space, it is proven that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed BUC(ℂⁿ) subalgebra symbols, can be linearly generated by Toeplitz operators with those symbols.  On the p-Bergman space, the Toeplitz algebras having BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) subalgebra symbols are studied, particularly near the boundary, where a result similar to that of the p=2 (the case for the unit disk) can be obtained with certain weighted l^p norm constraints on the symbols.

Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories without manual annotation, relying instead on simplified bounding-box labels, such as seatlings. However, these methods have inherent biases stemming from the base categories, limiting their performance in detecting novel object categories. In response, we have developed a framework, named ShadowDet, designed to mitigate the biases by introducing centerpoint predictions, such as object centers, as a supplementary regression target during training. Furthermore, we have found that incorporating information on the number of objects per image, known as object counts, is a cost-effective global pooling target that enhances inference quality by accurately estimating the number of objects in the image. Through comprehensive evaluations, we have demonstrated that ShadowDet sets a new standard in open-vocabulary object detection, outperforming existing methods by substantial margins while also achieving superior results on the COCO and VL-BERT datasets. The implementation details can be found at the website: https://yucecaner.github.io/ShadowDet/

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity that can be studied in great detail using high-resolution spectroscopy with the ESO ARCES and HARPS instruments. High-resolution spectra of direct continuum observations, as well as reconstructed images through interstellar absorption lines, reveal the distribution of ionized and atomic gas. Absorption from interstellar clouds, measured against photodissociation boundary objects and hydrogen reionization, provides information on the PDR's edge. Analyzing the blueshift of high-excitation lines in the PDR reveals gas outflows with orbital periods of 10-50 years. Moreover, the depth of absorption from interstellar clouds increases roughly with velocity as predicted by standard models of star-cloud interaction. However, the increase in absorption out of sight in standard models can be attributed to a small dense cloud on the PDR's edge, as well as the possible presence of a massive warm disk with a 1,000 AU radius that could be the source of the outflow. This warm disk could be the origin of gas moving at approximately 15 km/s, and its potential to influence the PDR.

The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text.
