Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions can significantly enhance 
learning under label noise. Prior studies examined global assumptions, such as 
symmetry, yet they do not consider local data patterns. Our work shows that 
local assumptions can, in fact, be more useful than their global counterparts, 
as they allow for wider ranges of noisy data to be learned. We focus on a specific 
local assumption - the knowledge of training example labels within a local 
neighborhood - and investigate its learnability in the most challenging scenario of 
constant label noise. Our findings indicate that local assumptions alone are 
insufficient for this scenario, but combining them with an even minimal amount of 
global data that lacks noise enables learning. Moreover, we compare a training 
algorithm based on local queries with its counterpart using random queries in the 
presence of various types of noise and finds that, not surprisingly, utilizing 
relevant local information yields better performance.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of the kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices. By showing that multiplying these matrices with vectors can be achieved in $O(N)$ operations and demonstrating their closure under specific operations like Hadamard product and matrix scaling, we resolved two critical challenges for IPOT complexity reduction. This breakthrough allows us to minimize the number of iterations, yielding the Fast Sinkhorn II algorithm, a method for computing optimal transport with low complexity and rapid convergence. Comprehensive numerical tests illustrate the success of our approach in achieving efficient computations.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two Jupiter-mass planets, can offer valuable insights into AU Mic b and c's evolution. Our 11-month study involves analyzing nearly 230 hours of Hubble Space Telescope's FUV data along with ground-based optical polarized flux data during flares, quiescence, and FUV/X-ray correlation. Resultant data reveal that AU Mic displays FUV radiation similar to that of other young stars, mainly resulting from the star's magnetic field rather than the planets. Our polarized optical flux observations imply that the star's magnetic field contains sufficient energy to support the FUV radiation observed, however, we also consider other possible explanations. Given the star's rapid X-ray fluctuations and FUV radiation, it appears that AU Mic's planets are unlikely to experience the most extreme effects predicted by theoretical models, primarily due to the presence of a potential corona or variations in stellar activity, which could provide a comparative framework for other young stars and exoplanets.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. We compare this description to a different model that has some similarities to the Landau-Lifshitz model and find that the other model exhibits non-physical behavior. Our new method suggests that the energy lost due to radiation will be limited by the energy lost due to mechanical resistance in the medium. We demonstrate that the critical velocity at which radiation friction equals mechanical resistance is around $10^{20}$ K, which is significantly higher than the average velocity of particles in a star. We provide estimates on how long it would take for a proton to slow down from a high velocity to this high friction velocity. We consider the impact of magnetic fields on our results and conclude that our new method is an reliable way to describe the friction caused by radiation when an object moves through a medium that undergoes mechanical resistance.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, making them vulnerable to these biases. The subgroup's excessive dominance tends to skew the predicted outcome, leading to incorrect predictions and potentially harmful forecastsknown as false positives. The impact of these mistakes is particularly pronounced in high-risk environments where such errors can cause severe consequences, like financial loss in the case of false alarm in healthcare. The widespread use of a simple k-Nearest-Neighbor classifier further exacerbates this problem. Our proposed research aims to mitigate this issue by proposing a novel, statistically-based method to neighbor selection in an unevenly distributed classification problems. The suggested neighborhood has the potential to minimize the occurrence of false positives and deliver more accurate forecasts. Thorough simulations utilizing artificially created datasets were conducted to compare the suggested algorithm against existing techniques. The results revealed that the proposed approach delivered considerable improvements in true positive rates and, more importantly, significant reductions in false positives. The statistical significance of these findings is easily interpretable and transparent for further modification if needed.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. By utilizing SkyMapper's DR3, along with 2MASS, VHS, and other datasets, we combine them with Euclid's PEP DR1 to derive the most complete photometry in the near-infrared region for QSOs with magnitudes above 19 at redshifts above 4.5. We then use this information to find 107 QSOs with the most extensive photometry available and 41 extremely bright QSOs with the most accurate magnitude readings. Among these, we particularly note the discovery of nine extremely bright QSOs with a magnitude of 19 or lower at redshifts above 6. To determine the distribution of QSOs at the luminous end, we conduct a simultaneous fit to the density of QSOs at a specific broad-line subclass and derive a slope and brightness value with an estimate of $b=-22.3^{+1.3}_{-1.5}$ and $\alpha=-2.52^{+0.13}_{-0.15}$. We obtained the results for a peak luminosity occurring at a magnitude of $M_{i}=-26.1^{+0.1}_{-0.2}$ with a slope of -22.3±1.3, but when including data from the Euclid's EMPS,

We have successfully observed and analyzed the charge-tunneling phenomena that occur between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our results show that these tunneling events can be accurately predicted based on the influence of environmental factors and the potential difference between the quantum dot and the superconducting island. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the quantum dot's state can be significantly affected even when it appears to be in a stable charge state due to the interference of multiple tunneling paths.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. Shockwaves that fit this classification and exhibit contractive properties are known as Lax-Friedrics and potential weak solutions to the system of equations, consisting of multiple conservation laws, are stable under certain conditions and satisfy the Lax-Friedrics condition. It has been previously proven that potential weak solutions, which are known to be stable under certain conditions and satisfy the Lax-Friedrics condition, converge over time to a stable equilibrium state. Building upon these findings, our research includes several contributions, which indicate that shockwaves with specific characteristics that do not fit the "stability" classification but still adhere to certain convexity requirements, also exhibit contractive behavior, which in turn implies that the sequence of approximate solutions converges towards a stable equilibrium over time.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training on internet-sourced nature scene images. Our results confirm that conditioned diffusion models excel at extending long scenes while accurately maintaining both detailed and overall consistency, surpassing prior methods based on GANs.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques like PCA and NCA to identify patterns in complex networks, focusing on applications to modeling, optimization, and control. Our method identifies the dominant patterns that capture a network's essential characteristics, allowing for reliable prediction and control of complex systems, even with limited data. It has been successfully demonstrated on various synthetic systems and the model of infectious disease SIS, outperforming other existing methods in prediction and design tasks.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of previous models is tested by applying them to certain conditions where they are valid, and their results are compared to numerical findings on the effect of slip on a liquid film.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation with Lipschitz bounds. Recently, B. Khoumeri and O. Burayou found that solutions of the equation are Lipschitz in its spatial variable when initial conditions are, and here we provide a proof that temporal Lipschitz stability holds under the same condition. Our key approach involves constructing a specific control function that generates a path toward the steady state. To tackle the challenge of Lipschitz dependence on time, we leverage a novel finite difference equation approximation of the equation that shares the temporal Lipschitz property with the original equation.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two independent observers reviewed the images and measured the cortical bone thickness and intervertebral disc thickness in both coronal and sagittal planes. The results showed strong agreement between robotic and manual scans in terms of spinous process angle, cortical bone thickness, and intervertebral disc thickness, with intraclass correlation coefficients ranging from 0.65 to 0.80. Slight discrepancies between robotic and manual measurements were observed, with mean differences of 0.2-1.0 mm. Notably, robotic scanning yielded more consistent measurements among observers, with mean differences reducing by 60-80%. These findings support the use of robotic scanning as a reliable assessment tool for determining the spinal curvature in scoliosis patients.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate word transition probabilities and frame duration correlations. Using a median-based output and a non-parametric approach, this approach avoids assumptions made by traditional continuous probability distributions. As a result, it offers the ability to model duration data at any resolution without fragmentation and can also detect and warn of data irregularities during training. Additionally, this method can be used with any time series and can be combined with population-level distributional information in conjunction with local information. An evaluation of this method using Nihongobed showed positive results in terms of modelling frame-level duration variability and when combined with word-level probabilities, it further enhanced accuracy.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for our 'MixNet' framework to facilitate feature sharing among subnetworks, resulting in more synchronized predictions and improved overall performance. Conversely, we illustrate that existing MIMO frameworks can prevent feature sharing by isolating subnetworks and compromising their combined model performance. Our research applies these insights to a smartphone with limited hardware capabilities, demonstrating that our unsupervised 'unmixing' procedure can enhance MIMO ensemble performance without increasing parameters.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of historical document image datasets
from diverse collections across the globe. It scrutinizes each dataset's characteristics
such as illustration prevalence, page layout, languages employed, time periods covered,
page counts, total images, and any accompanying ground data, while also providing
access to a standardized data catalog linking relevant information with respective
datasets. Additionally, this work catalogues datasets using established descriptors
such as the Institute of the Information Technology in Brussels Dataset Description
format, thereby facilitating effective dataset sharing in the future.

Due to their versatility and low cost, modular robots have become an appealing choice for many industrial and research settings. However, their research applications are currently limited to basic tasks such as pick-and-place measurements. This study aims to expand the scope of modular robots in research by implementing them in Markov Decision Process-driven tasks that require precise movement prediction. A novel prediction-based method known as flatness error control is developed to accurately position the robot's mechanical arm, yielding minimal predictions of ${0.12}^{0.5}$ mm in a 6D space. To achieve this accuracy, two precision sensors are integrated at a minimal cost, one placed on the transmission lever and the other attached to an actuator load. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in pinpointing precise positions, even in the presence of external influences that might disrupt movement.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which involve analyzing various aspects of a person's social life, our proposed method aims to assess multiple aspects of an individual's health trajectory. This may involve studying the dynamics of a person's health over time, the variation in these dynamics across different time periods, the effect of specific events or changes on these dynamics, and the simultaneous analysis of multiple individuals' health trajectories. To achieve this, our approach utilizes the MSA4R R package to perform a multidimensional analysis of lifecourse trajectories using the generalized linear advanced mixed (GLAM) model, which allows for the simultaneous assessment of four distinct aspects. Our method is demonstrated through an analysis of Adenine, a simulation-based package, output. This is followed by an application of the methodology in an analysis of the lifecourse trajectories of patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction, utilizing data from the GENDHIE study.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site and calculates integrals through a weighted average of the potential based on the distance to the nearest nucleus. This weighted average is known to preserve the correct value of integrals for spherical functions, but it is proven here to be incorrect for the more relevant Gaussian functions, where the effective distance of a Gaussian orbit is the mean of the Gaussian and the center position. In addition to this, the method is capable of evaluating integrals related to an atomic basis set through an analytical formula derived from a second-order expansion of the potential around the base point, an approach known as the Pontisio-Sadlej method. This method is capable of evaluating all electronic integrals with respect to coordinates and basis functions, but it is incorrect for functions that decline slowly over distance. Combining the two approaches, a new analytical formula is developed, blending the multi-center scheme with the Pontisio-Sadlej method, and it is correct for all electronic integrals, thereby resulting in an algorithm with high efficiency.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of a given size involves determining the minimum size of such a set, which is referred to as the dimension of the graph. When an instance of this problem includes additional constraints, it becomes a parameterized problem, which can be solved efficiently for certain parameter values. The problem is parameterized by several structural parameters, including feedback vertex sets, which are known to have a linear parameter upper bound, but may actually have a much smaller parameter upper bound. The problem is also parameterized by vertex cover and can be solved efficiently under certain conditions. The problem of distance constraints with vertices also involves determining if a subset of vertices (the target set) can be connected to a set of special vertices (the transversal set) such that distances between the two sets and between the vertices of the target set are all constrained within a given range, which is a new problem and can be solved with a given size constraint. The problem of graph finding a resolving set (the resolving subgraph) and can be solved for the case when the size of the resolving set and some structural parameters are used as limits. The problem of graph (the strong resolving subgraph) and can be solved for certain size and structural parameters. The problem of graph (the path covering problem) and can be solved for certain size and structural parameters

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to high atmospheric heating, research has suggested this could lead to reduced precipitation, but these precipitation patterns have not been extensively studied. To bridge this gap, our study uses climate simulation models to investigate 'hothouse' climates and their predicted precipitation behaviors. Notably, we discovered a precipitation increase below a certain altitude and a more significant decrease above it in response to low atmospheric heating. Moreover, 'hothouse' climates exhibit intense precipitation events more often and to a greater extent than modern climates, with significant implications for our understanding of precipitation patterns in 'hothouse' environments.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin extensions of Yang-Mills theory, a phenomenon also evident in a self-contained unitary setting. This action is characterised by an infinite set of massless three-form gauge fields, each accompanied by their respective gauge symmetries. We've also outlined a systematic procedure for constructing three-form gauge fields and their associated external field counterparts.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust and reliable models from noisy medical image data presents a significant challenge. To tackle this problem, we've devised a novel method incorporating Bayesian statistics to counterbalanced label noise. The proposed model employs an advanced labeling mechanism that utilizes latent knowledge derived from disease statistics to determine the likelihood of correct patient diagnoses. The model's output is adjusted based on this statistical analysis to accurately reflect the underlying disease distribution. Experimental evaluation on multiple medical image datasets has shown that the proposed method provides an optimal balance between reducing overfitting and mitigating the impact of noisy labels, outperforming existing approaches.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. A positive number, $C_0$, is stated whose existence proves that the norm of $P$ does not exceed $C_0$ for any function in $C(Q_n)$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and it is proven that the stochastic matrix of the CRW, corresponding to a vertex v, has a characteristic polynomial of (x - 1) φ(G, x), where φ(G, x) is the characteristic polynomial of the Grover matrix of walk from vertex v.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of instantaneously occurring wall-bound flows is heavily reliant on the geometric characteristics of the representative elements used in the analysis. This requires a precise understanding of the shape and dimensionality of these elements, particularly the nano-scale elements which have not been previously quantified. By employing advanced imaging techniques, our research has revealed that nano-scale elements exhibit a high degree of variability and asymmetry, which cannot be accurately represented by current geometric models. This discrepancy significantly impacts the accuracy of models attempting to quantify these features, resulting in substantial inaccuracies in terms of timing, magnitude, and spatial interrelation. By incorporating the newly discovered information into a modified model framework, our research has demonstrated an approximate 50% reduction in prediction inaccuracy, bringing it more inline with measured data. This has important implications for incorporating this type of modelling into computational simulations used for informing industrial-scale engineering designs with the aim of improving aerodynamic and friction properties.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld terms. Notably, this model is entirely self-contained, as it does not rely on the presence of external background fields. An approximate solution to the combined equation for the Skyrme bilinear and Born-Infeld density is derived for small values of the Born-Infeld parameter, after which the self-dual equations are solved approximately. Furthermore, the study includes a quantization of the system, revealing an increase in its classical action due to the Born-Infivid term, yet also observes that the approximate solution developed previously remains a viable configuration for the self-dual equations.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p$ times $\frac{2\pi\hbar}{2p}$, we identify key phase transitions. When $p$ is an integer or half-integer, the semimetal phase transitions into a band insulating phase, whereas for rational values of $p$ that cannot be reduced to integers or halves, the semimetal phase persists at infinitely high magnetic strength. Furthermore, even at high magnetic strength, it is possible for certain values of $p$ to have multiple topological invariants non-zero, leading to the absence of a larger bandgap between the two groups of pairs of Weyl nodes and the inverse semimetal phase. This results in an increase of the bandgap size between these invariants groups and the mentioned inverse semimetal phase, which may lead to two new gapped topological phases emerging for rational values of $p$.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional photons when subjected to optical stimulation. The structure features a narrow 10-nanometer gap separating a gold mirror from the nanoring and quantum dots, enabling efficient interaction between the quantum dots and the dual modes supported by the setup - resonant gap modes and radiative antenna modes. Our experimental findings confirm that the quantum dots within the nanogap can efficiently couple to these modes to enhance the absorption of the stimulating light and emit light with high directionality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adjusting simple geometric parameters, such as the outer and inner diameters of the nanoring, allows us to independently tune the resonance spectral positions of the setup. This unique property allows us to achieve average fluorescence enhancements of up to 654 times in combination with a high radiation efficiency and a narrow cone of directional emission ($\pm 17^\circ$) perpendicular to the sample surface.

Mechanical screening, a widely observed phenomenon, can also occur in granular
assemblies where stress concentrations are disseminated throughout the system
by particle deformation. Researchers previously proposed an "anomalous screening
hypothesis" suggesting that mechanical stress is disseminated in granular
assemblies depending on the distance static particles are from each other. The
hy-pothesis claims that stress only decreases when the distance between static
particles minimizes gradients in the stress tensor. Theoretical models used to
develop this concept, known as "pressure-pressure correlation functions",
have not been extensively tested or validated. In the present study, the authors
measure stress relaxation in granular columns made of soft static particles following
an external stress load displacement. Researchers also used numerical models based
on discrete particle simulations to confirm these results. Data and findings were
compared to established theories such as the jammed state pressure-pressure
correlation functions and relaxation models derived from the Frankel-Narayan-
Langer (FNL) pressure-pressure correlation functions, leading to the conclusion
that these stress models decrease at rates proportional to distance raised to
the power of 2, consistent with numerical and experimental observations in this
study.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with its age estimation. Estimating the supernova's distance from Earth ranges between 8-20 kiloparsecs or approximately 26-66 thousand light-years. A thorough examination of potential Type Ia or core-collapse supernovae explosions has been conducted, including simulations of the latter's properties. These show that a 10^32 erg event could develop into a ~20 parsec sized, 20 solar mass young star, consistent with infrared observations. A scan of the surrounding molecular cloud has identified a likely explosion site, about 2 parsecs from Sgr A East. This points to a core-collapse supernova, with a radius expansion lasting 3000 years and an estimated explosion energy of 10^32-10^33 erg. Compared to other recent supernova predictions, this suggests the progenitor star was around 10 solar masses, with a potential black hole remnant of approximately 1.4 to 5.5 solar masses. Mass transfer from a companion could have fueled the star's final years, with a proposed binary system described.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of three novel techniques: one that generates data based on the mode of class distributions, another that detects natural breaks in the data sequence, and a random-press technique. The new methods are tested against three established oversampling methods. The findings reveal that the mode-based and natural-break methods outperformed others, with the random-press method also showing promise in limited context. The proposed techniques are set to enhance the efficiency of classifying text data.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct approach and platform compared to existing research, we focus on one minute, issue-level data from 577 U.S. outlets between April 2020 and February 2021. Our results indicate that local news outlets in the U.S. initially covered COVID at a rate closely linked to regional COVID case rates. Following the January 2021 U.S. election, local news coverage of COVID increased in high-case areas, but this growth was not correlated with COVID case and death rates. We found no evidence suggesting outlets covering COVID at a higher rate also received greater audience attention. These findings enable a more accurate comparison of local news COVID coverage with national and state-level reports.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, ensuring angular momentum conservation remains unaltered. Furthermore, we have alleviated the perceivable 25% momentum scattering artifact, which transitioned into a 0.05 % drift in momentum (angular momentum) when particles experience high velocities (binary system orbital velocity), thereby ensuring total momentum/angular momentum conservation in line with the system initial conditions. We have illustrated the outcome of this advancement using a binary merger simulation, which displayed no residual drifts, thereby ensuring Conserved initial conditions.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully polarized, in-line initial and final protons have been carried out to analyze polarization transfer and compare results to an experiment measuring double-spin asymmetry in another process. Research found a significant $Q^2$ dependence influence on a particular polarization tensor component and found that a certain tensor contribution varies significantly with $Q^2$ compared to a comparable calculation using the Born approximation. This $Q^2$ dependence also impacts polarization transfer to the proton, with a significant share of polarization coming from the GAChYR mechanism, specifically its GA and HY components. This indicates a complex $Q^2$ dependence influencing polarization transfer, indicating a need for detailed calculations rather than simplified approximations.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. In this context, we introduce AugPC, a policy cloning framework that achieves exactness at a fraction of the cost and efficiency as its theoretical maximum, thereby enabling the training of multiple, sequential models on the same environment using the same hardware. To achieve this, we utilize techniques from optimal control theory, embedding a pivotal factor within a compact, finite-dimensional subspace that allows us to precisely replicate the expert model's transition and reward characteristics. As a result, our method empowers the simultaneous training of numerous, highly accurate imitation agents on the same hardware that would be insufficient for training a single, comparable agent using max accuracy settings. Our approach also extends to the imitation learning setting where we compare our method to state-of-the-art techniques and demonstrate that policy cloning can achieve superior precision at lower cost and runtime in a wide range of environments involving both discrete and continuous actions.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other charged particles, and each Higgs boson ($h$) into two jets of particles or into a bottom quark and associated jet of particles. The investigation aims to detect the $Vhh$ signals representing critical components of both the Standard Model and various proposed physics beyond existing understanding. The study utilizes a statistical threshold of expected and observed occurrence of 0.8 and 0.85 times the likelihood expectation for the vector boson ($Z$ to electrons and neutrinos) combined with 0.07 and 0.1 times the vector boson ($W$ to electrons and neutrinos) combined expectation for the $Vhq\bar{q}$ or $\mathrm{b}\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ decay modes of the Higgs bosons.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by aliasing, can integrate digital signal processing directly into their design, eliminating external modulation requirements. This integration of digital and atomic systems enables the development of a more stable and responsive system, allowing for increased precision when measuring magnetic field gradients and timelines. Our study demonstrates a high-resolution maser output using this combined technology, capable of achieving an extremely high coherence, decoupling the digital processing from the sensitive atomic detector, and resulting in high-quality maser output even in challenging environments.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model by introducing a U(1) global symmetry, where a specific parameter range is presented, and, most notably, amenable to experimental verification, particularly through the observation of secondary gamma-ray production in the Milky Way's center, via the annihilation of a neutralino pair, and, additionally, by examining the Sun's electromagnetic detection of such decaying particles.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks in this context mean that each major component consists of highly interconnected sub-groups of vertices. The method employs a randomized algorithmic approach that efficiently reduces complex surface topography aspects while maintaining accurate vertex mapping without distorting key network structure features. The algorithm provides a precise surface topology mapping with a guaranteed error rate of less than 2, with a computational time directly proportional to the number of vertices. Despite running efficiently, this approach becomes impractically resource-intensive for very large datasets. Unfortunately, we found it impossible to develop an adaptive surface mapping method (one that automatically finds the best possible surface topography for each given network without overfitting to random patterns) that meets our desired performance standards. Consequently, we developed a different approach - a Fast Approximation Scheme with randomly assigned surface topography maps, yielding a computationally efficient result at the expense of potentially inaccurate surface topology representations in the context of large datasets.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. Directly measuring this direction with high precision can provide the means to determine the dark matter velocity distribution and resolve the neutrino oscillation problem if electron scattering events can also be accurately measured. Recent advancements in technology, particularly with Micro-Channel Photo-Detectors in Time-Projection Chambers, have made it easier to achieve this level of identification. Due to their common use as dark matter detectors and neutrino detectors, it's essential to develop methods that don't rely on the reporting of likelihood ratios. Instead, being able to define specific sets of observations that definitely or definitely don't correspond to light-mass dark matter, will improve the performance of next-generation experiments. By using simulated data of low-ionization Recoil-Electron Pair events in a 1 kg-SCALE gas detector operating at atmospheric pressure, this study demonstrates a method for identifying recoil direction by using meta-data from electron drift trajectories. These meta-data include the electron collection time and its ionization energy through drift velocity. Using a drift field of 0.15 Tesla/m, electrons generated 0.5 cm from the detector's end are completely collected in 30 microseconds, providing sufficient statistics to identify this local ionization spot even when the recoil location is uniformly distributed across the active volume, provided the electron mean drift time is measured with an accuracy of two nanoseconds.
