A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert Integrated Decision-making, involving human experts in the decision-making process. This approach utilizes deep learning to enhance decision-makers' objectivity and fairness by detecting bias and providing real-time context information. As the integrity of automated decision-making processes comes under scrutiny, our proposed method offers a pioneering model for trustworthy AI-assisted decision-making in complex scenarios.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The proposed benchmark and code are designed for ease of use and can be accessed at https://github.com/multimodalai/oov_challenge.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about these fields' dynamic behaviors, with most research focusing on their first and second statistical properties. To better understand living systems and develop more accurate models, researchers have been seeking a framework that goes beyond standard probability theory. We propose a novel approach based on geodesic curves in the context of Gaussian random field manifolds. By applying this method, we can determine the optimal trajectory between two points, avoiding the unneeded computation of second moment properties. We demonstrate that this technique allows for the identification of a random field's geometric structure and provide a geometric interpretation of geodesics. Additionally, we present a simulation example and discuss its potential applications in the field of system biology.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar outcome applies to the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights in contact with normal and spin-up and spin-down electrons. The findings demonstrated that with gate modulation, these systems can be tuned for high spin polarization, rendering them suitable for spintronics applications. The ability to control barrier heights using gate voltage also allows for the realization of spin-dependent bandgap scenarios, where spin polarization reaches its maximum. Additionally, the team discovered that even in bandgap states, spin-dependent transport is possible with appropriate barrier heights. The understanding of spin-dependent transport in these systems could enable the development of more spin-based devices.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by various examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number at the center of certain graph theories. In the present paper, we improve upon this statement by showing that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 25 to the fourth power and an independence number of five will always contain all cycles from three to twenty-five. A supplementary result reveals that a graph on n vertices with an independence number of five and hamiltonian cycles will still contain all cycles, provided the length of the cycles does not exceed one-third of n.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at an energy of 200 GeV was studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the formation of a quark-gluon plasma, and found that the direction of light particles emitted indicates the formation of a quark-gluon plasma, however, the impact of viscosity in certain directions resulted in minimal deviation from average behavior. This research also established a correlation between nuclear overcharge and trajectory of light particles. A quantitative assessment of nuclear overcharge was found to be relatively stable in certain scenarios and correlated with a variable indicating QGP viscosity. This research found that the formation of a quark-gluon plasma in heavy nuclei results in a variable QGP viscosity of approximately 0.1 to several units across various energy levels.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across diverse scientific and engineering fields. Despite its high accuracy, ASK has a computational disadvantage in dealing with multi-dimensional systems compared to traditional integration methods like Runge-Kutta. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach that combines the ASK method with sparse grid techniques to speed up computation for high-dimensional systems. This hybrid method, sparse-grid-based ASK, utilizes the Smolyak structure to efficiently construct collocation points and associated polynomials that help approximate Koopman operator eigenfunctions. By reducing the number of collocation points compared to traditional tensor product methods, SASK offers improved computational efficiency without compromising accuracy. Numerical simulations demonstrate that SASK achieves an optimal balance between accuracy and computational cost, thus accelerating ASK. Furthermore, SASK's capabilities can also be extended to solve partial differential equations in their semi-discrete form.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on the challenge of simulating ionization processes in atoms and molecules exposed to intense external electric fields. It primarily focuses on the early developments from a theoretical perspective, with supporting experimental frameworks. The discussion starts with the description of a pivotal measurement that identified the need for a quantum mechanical theory to describe ionized states of atoms and molecules in fields. It then introduces the concept of exterior complex scaling as a potential solution to simulate ionized states and outlines its theoretical implementation. The review concludes by discussing recent advancements where DC fields interact with nuclei in substances that exhibit superconductivity and ferromagnetism.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's known that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, the opposite scenario has received less attention. This paper examines what happens when no solution exists by introducing two new problems. One problem demands that distances to a set of target points, under a specific norm, be met as closely as possible. The other problem involves minimizing a Lagrangoid with respect to these target points. It's discovered that the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to the solution of the Lagrangoid problem when no solution exists. However, convergence requires that the margin parameter $\varepsilon$ approach zero from above. A key challenge arises from non-uniqueness of solutions to the Lagrangoid problem, as well as difficulties in differentiating its value. These obstacles are overcome through the introduction of two new properties and the proof of their applicability in this scenario. The properties enable modification of the Sinkhorn algorithm, first by proving its monotonous convergence towards stationary points of the Lagrangoid, and second by establishing its differentiability at every interior point.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% following a calculation of statistical and systematic uncertainties. The measurement is compared with the Standard Model prediction, showing no notable deviations.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system influence an entrapped particle's behavior. This is particularly true in cases where the surrounding system undergoes significant changes. For instance: (i) A particle trapped within a potential that's itself bound to a moving harmonic oscillator will oscillate locally in the oscillator's natural frequency. (ii) When the surrounding system behaves erratically, representing an ergodic dynamical network, the entrapped particle will adopt a disordered state marked by its position being completely uncertain. (iii) Should the surrounding system possess a minimal amount of coherence and coherence fluctuations, the entrapped particle will experience prolonged localized periods at specific positions. This phenomenon stems from an entrapped particle's ground state transferring coherently into other states.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-convex and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ 
to be Janowski convex as well as $z{u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be Janowski starlike in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions. Studies have found that the agglomeration benefits of cities can be measured by the number of individuals that pass through them in a given period. Disruption to urban life due to the COVID-19 pandemic led to residents altering their behavior in an effort to limit its spread, including reducing social contacts and maintaining spatial distance in public. As a result, residents lost the advantage that urban diversity would normally provide. Our findings are based on simulated urban encounters that considered various productivities across different areas of London. We found that the COVID-19 related change in behavior not only eliminated the agglomeration benefits of diversity but also resulted in a negative value, indicating that the diversity of urban encounters had a negative impact on income. However, we also discovered that the COVID-19 outbreak led to a decrease in the variety of urban encounters but did not affect their homogeneity. The data used in this study was collected from over 155,000 London residents and includes their addresses, professions and places of employment. The findings suggest that the COVID-19 pandemic had a negative economic impact by increasing the concentration of a limited number of individuals in urban centers.)

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied at the preconditioned state via system linearization.
Using demanding case studies, simulation results indicate that this algorithm can
exceed the performance of conventional strategies, like Full Monte Carlo multiphase
model simulation, with favorable outcomes even in the presence of extreme grid
resource constraints. Further details about this investigation are documented within
the accompanying ARX module.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric and non geometric structures from atoms to complex living organisms, reflecting their intrinsic asymmetry. Chiral matter responds differently to circularly polarized light of the same direction compared to its opposite counterpart, leading to a variety of optical phenomena. We propose and evaluate chirally confined optical cavities consisting of a mirror coated with a chiral metasurface, capable of supporting unidirectional propagation of circularly polarized light within the cavity. The integration of polarization-dependent transmission and reflection coefficients from chiral thin films into the Fabry-Perot cavity analysis enables the theoretical examination of unidirectional lasing and the efficient emission of light with a specific handedness.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. We also derive the boundary Schwarzian theory from the Liouville CFT and further establish an equivalence between the two-dimensional string theory and a specific time-dependent matrix model. This relation is then generalized to the case of two-dimensional de-Sitter JT gravity.

A spacetime metric, known as the warp drive solution, has been proposed but remains incomplete due to a severe astrophysical obstruction, rendering stars impossible to warp. Research discovered that by introducing a perfect fluid with pressure density and bulk viscosity as the sole matter field in Einstein's general relativity, these obstacles are overcome, enabling the formation of warp drive solutions that coexist with Einstein's cosmological constant. This theoretical framework has led to two new metrics, where the Einstein equations are satisfied, allowing warp drive effects to occur in these spacetimes.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process the data generated from excavations - thereby providing cities with a valuable resource for assessing and planning their infrastructure. This paper presents the GUIDES framework, a systematic and automated solution for mapping and processing excavations' spatial data. This data is subsequently utilized for generating various types of information - including the infrastructure's spatial distribution, areas with high risk for pipe collisions and cost estimates for new constructions. Our tests have shown that GUIDES can accurately detect new constructions' locations and calculate the costs associated with different construction methods.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a 2D Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the characterization of their transverse movement. This was done by comparing the experimentally measured effects on spin dephasing with theoretical predictions, resulting in accurate estimations of temperature levels consistent with previously documented standards, including both laser cooling constraints and earlier research methods. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that the primary source of noise affecting the ions' movement is the laser beam's spatial intensity variation.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our novel quantum mechanical approach simplifies this task by incorporating the effects of light and electromagnetic interactions between the tip and sample into standalone quantum mechanical calculations. These calculations can be effortlessly combined with existing software to produce detailed and chemically specific images of surfaces. Our method is supported by several real-world examples, including simulations of CO molecules and are compared to experimental results, with consistent alignment of chemical and physical signals. This method allows for a link to be established between experimentally determined spectra and specific molecular transitions, ultimately enabling more precise identification of molecules through comparison to extensive databases.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find excess emission due to AME beyond the expected thermal and synchrotron component contributions. Instead of the expected increase in emission at 18.6 GHz, we noticed a decrease in relation to the thermal contribution; similar results were found for the adjacent galaxies, revealing that the thermal component dominates and no significant AME signal is present. For M 31, we found significant excess emission at 24.6 GHz which cannot be fully explained by the expected thermal and synchrotron components, although its properties still require further confirmation. Our non-detection in the observed galaxies' fields using a Bayesian approach sets an upper limit on 4'F$_\nu$ (Jy kpc$^{-2}$) at 18.6 GHz ($3.43\pm1.64$), 24.6 GHz ($1.35\pm0.65$), 32.8 GHz ($0.99\pm0.48$),

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. Simulations reveal the underlying causes of these properties stem from the direct interaction between the ammonium ion's electric dipole and the lattice polarization, influenced by hydrogen bonding, which also explains the 65% entropy loss during the phase transition.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy to achieve the highest rewards, but this suboptimal approach can sometimes lead to better outcomes than making the optimal choice every time. The capacity to switch between optimal and suboptimal methods is thought to be a characteristic that helps us adapt to changing situations, yet people often stick to a less than optimal strategy to achieve the highest rewards, which indicates that there's a trade-off between exploring new methods and benefiting from what we already know. By investigating a learning task called the "Causal Association Learning Task", we found that individuals who adopted a strategy that balances exploring new methods and benefiting from what they already know showed a stronger connection between the brain's error signal and new expectations, which indicates a more adaptive learning process. The error signal is thought to be the driver of this adaptive learning process, which is supported by our results, however the underlying mechanisms that govern this process are still not fully understood and require further investigation. The results from our experiments provide novel insights that could help us develop more advanced algorithms for machines that learn and help us understand the world better.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate Swedlund-Pyk and Kane-Broderson's experiments, and its dual could be used to run Swedlund-Pyk's experiment twice a day with 40 particles, and Kane and Broderson's experiment twice a day with 8 particles, both of which would yield key distributions outside the set of all possible key distributions for two players. Furthermore, it's suggested that setting the phase according to Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen's correlation could serve as quantum cryptography, and that hitting exact correlations might allow for non-computable data after reading it, which could serve as quantum concealment and concealment verification tools.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the previously best result for an improved approximation factor while also reaching the previously best result with reduced query complexity. Additionally, lower bounds on the data structure's efficiency were derived using the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis.

The growth in the complexity of quantum information processing is heavily dependent on progress in quantum computing hardware. One major constraint is set by the accuracy of measurement instruments. Researchers have developed various methods to correct for measurement inaccuracies, although the current techniques are mainly limited by storage capacity rather than processing speed. We've developed a new approach called iterative Bayesian unfolding that efficiently mitigates measurement errors without increasing computational demands. This method accurately reproduces data without discarding it and has no predefined limitations. We've successfully tested our approach on simulated data and real-world experiments, confirming its efficacy in correcting measurement errors. Furthermore, our approach can also be used for noise reduction.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on "shared autonomy" focuses on developing methods for making robotic interpretations of human intent precise. Despite this, past work on refining robotic interpretations lacks a clear understanding of how these adjustments impact the quality of the resulting task. We introduce a novel approach, using a task-convention model, to assess and refine robotic interpretations by measuring the conventions (e.g., object manipulation techniques) the robot learns and applies. By incorporating the new method into a closed-loop system, our results demonstrate that the quality of the resulting task and the robot's accuracy in inferring human intent both significantly improve.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map to serve as key navigation landmarks, enabling the system to stay on track and correcting its position when the map is integrated. During testing, HiTMap demonstrated its efficacy in unknown environments when compared to a prominent state-of-the-art navigation approach, showcasing its ability to accurately find its way using its map and detecting frontiers, ultimately resulting in minimal position drift.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D synchronization, and phased array antennas. This paper explores the use of multivariable functions to create inter-group complementary code sets and 2-D Z-Complementary Array Code Sets. To achieve this, two potential sets based on multivariable functions, namely the unitary multivariable functions set AMF(n, m, k, l) and the non-unitary multivariable functions set BMF(n, m, k, l), are identified and analyzed. By establishing the two possible forms of multivariable functions, the paper demonstrates the potential use of AMF and BMF to generate inter-group complementary code sets and 2-D Z-Complementary Array Code Sets, respectively. Furthermore, the paper examines the statistical properties of AMF and BMF, and proposes a method to construct these sets and arrays. This approach offers a novel and reliable solution for constructing inter-group complementary code sets and 2-D Z-Complementary Array Code Sets.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the multiple energy levels may not only serve to improve image clarity but also provide information about specific tissue types or materials. However, the limited number of sensor readings often introduces significant noise, which can impede image analysis. In this study, we introduce a novel variational formulation that can distinguish between different materials, remove noise caused by the sensor, and accurately capture the effects of X-ray beam hardening. The model employs a unique and mathematically consistent representation of polyenergetic X-rays, employs a non-convex regularizer that incorporates information about material transitions, and incorporates an additional term that incorporates data from a limited number of clean sensor readings to remove noise. The model's parameters are optimized through a combination of the alternating direction method of multi-variables and the Davidon\(-\)Bertsekas technique. The model's effectiveness is confirmed through experiments using polyenergetic magnetic resonance tomography data, x-ray computed tomography data containing a variety of materials, and laboratory-based material measurement equipment.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as unbounded fields and unconnected light patterns. Notably, the desirable results from the hydrodynamics model can be attributed to two separate factors - the gradual reduction of spillover effects and the exponential decay of nonlocal effects with decreasing gap sizes.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that when users' inputs are factored in, significant boosts in recall rates can be achieved, with a high of 61% improvement observed. CERN's effectiveness also surpasses competitors in both automated and user-driven settings. Within CNER, our work in Named Entity Retrieval (NER) shows that incorporating term-level user input yields higher accuracy rates, with a maximum improvement of 26%. Notably, our research in CNER highlights the importance of involving users in the process and provides the foundations for gathering user feedback in this field.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and detailed daily patterns, all linked over various time spans. In contrast, longitudinal data often involves fewer variables and is typically observed over a more extended period, sometimes spanning decades. This type of data is frequently characterized by longitudinal trends, gradual changes over time, and infrequent frequent measurements. Both types of data can be challenging to visualize and analyze due to their complexity, and they often benefit from the examination of aggregate patterns and trends, as well as from the exploration of their individual components. Researchers and analysts in these domains place significant reliance on data visualization as an essential component of their investigative processes, and they typically follow a systematic approach of progressive exploration, starting with high-level aggregate views, and then delving deeper into specific sub-components and details. However, this structured process typically requires significant data management and handling across various temporal scales and relatedness levels that are often incompatible with interactive data visualizations. This paper discusses the concepts and approaches that address these challenges, focusing on the ability to connect various scales and observe data over time, and it outlines methodologies for managing and structuring time-based multivariate and longitudinal data, while maintaining a high degree of interactivity.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in making more accurate diagnoses and reducing mortality rates. Advances in recent years have seen the development of sequential or graph-based models aiming to tackle this goal. Despite the complexity and diversity of EHR data, which can be visualized as a multi-layered, interconnected network (heterogeneous graph), past studies have neglected these essential aspects. Moreover, existing methods that deal with graph diversity are not directly applicable to EHR data due to its unique properties such as the presence of dominant hub nodes. To address this limitation, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel technique that leverages graph neural networks to effectively analyze EHR data. Our approach consists of a dual-module architecture, which synthesizes global and local similarity matrices. Our empirical studies conducted on real-world datasets showcase the superior performance of HSGNN in comparative settings against prominent baselines.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we analyze the influence of surface fluctuation, electrolyte concentration, and solvent polarization on the distribution of ions and water near the surface, as well as the contact value rule. We find that solvent effects significantly impact the ion and water density profiles, particularly at high electrolyte concentrations where the outer Helmholtz plane moves farther away from the surface. Furthermore, we find that solvent effects cause a displacement of the inner Helmholtz plane and modify the ion distribution within the electric double layer. Our study provides a framework for modeling the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material in the presence of solvent polarization.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and evaluated its practicality for automating this process by comparing it to human performance on two identical tasks. The results showed that the model's accuracy is currently limited, but our findings provide valuable insights for advancing this research area.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify it, then a two-stage algorithm is proposed to solve it, consisting of a schedule determination algorithm that utilizes a lower bound of energy efficiency to find an optimal schedule, and a power allocation algorithm that allocates power to each link in the most energy-efficient manner possible. A comparison with a timing-based power control strategy using numerical results shows that this method yields higher energy efficiency than a timing-based power control strategy under the same outage probability constraint.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific information includes the impact of local spin-exchange interactions, the characteristics of the host material's density of states, and the magnetic impurity's hybridization with neighboring atoms. A key finding of this approach is that magnetic moments on the impurity may not remain unchanged and could degenerate into smaller magnetic moments, known as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, at low concentration. This theoretical framework has been successfully tested through comparison with experimental data obtained from high-resolution magnetic imaging of individual magnetic impurities, such as an Mn adatom and Mn dimers, placed on the Nb(110) surface. A related method has also been introduced to identify local moments that arise within non-magnetic superconductors as a result of exchange field-induced spin-polarization. Preliminary results indicate that magnetic moments remain intact at high concentration but undergo a transition to degenerate states at low concentration, similar to what is observed in dilute magnetic impurities, with the potential to be realized through scanning tunneling spectroscopy and magnetic imaging.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) and Fast-NDT (FNDT) are widely employed for shape alignment in various fields. They are particularly valued to account for positional biases which can introduce errors in measurements, for instance, in both the source and target shapes being slightly offset doesn't impact their effectiveness. Nonetheless, in many cases, implementing data filtering to reduce positional bias prior to application is necessary. This research presents a novel filter that utilizes a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to mitigate positional bias prior to the NDT and FNDT algorithms. The proposed DNN filter with NDT and FNDT showed significant accuracy improvements, specifically with (1) reducing the mean bias to less than a millimeter using the NDT and (2) achieving an average point-to-point registration error of 0.046 meters using the FNDT on a dataset consisting of 8980 points from various outdoor scenes.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently accelerated the analysis of satellite imagery. 
Although deep learning methods deliver superior edge detection at a lower 
computational cost compared to traditional approaches, they necessitate substantial 
storage space and are limited by their large size. Moreover, deep learning methods 
require specialized hardware, such as Graphics Processing Units, to function 
efficiently. This paper presents a novel edge detection algorithm tailored for 
satellite images that runs on standard hardware without requiring excessive 
storage. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance is comparable to the latest 
deep learning and traditional techniques, while consistently delivering 
consistent results for various datasets.

Subjecting solid materials to a high-energy electron beam prompts a range of intricate processes, including the generation of voids, defect production, and energy dissipation. These effects trigger collective changes in the material's interaction with the impinging electron flux, which has a substantial impact on the resulting X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra observed. This research provides a detailed rate model for modeling changes to the electron population and XANES response over time as the electron flux and total electron dose increase. The model incorporates the concepts of void annihilation, defect saturation, and energy dissipation. Simulation results demonstrate excellent correlation with experimental XANES data for carbon and titanium materials hit by high-energy electron pulses.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN countermeasures have been compromised by our research, which is the first to tackle this specific type of attack for AMC systems. Experiments using signals from four types of modulation (BPSK, QPSK, QAM-4, and QAM-8) showed that our method is highly effective against adversarial attacks in wireless channels.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it's exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We examine the potential of
experience replay, a notable method in the field of artificial intelligence,
specifically within the context of segmenting lesions using imaging data from 8
different hospitals. Our experiments confirm that experience replay achieves a
beneficial effect by preserving previously acquired knowledge, while reducing
the likelihood of forgetting previous lessons compared to sequential fine-tuning.
Notably, our study also shows that experience replay outperforms training on
multiple domains, solidifying its status as a potential solution for the
challenging task of segmenting MS lesions. A related repository containing the
code used for the study can be accessed here:
https://github.com/naga-karthik/continual-learning-ms

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data. To tackle this, we've developed an integrated framework that combines data-driven learning and domain knowledge to identify complex systems even with limited, noisy observations. This framework can be applied to different machine learning models, both continuous and discrete, and handles different types of model errors. 

Firstly, we've explored the impact of a specific type of error that isn't influenced by past events and proved that the accuracy of predictions is closely tied to the duration of the training data. 

For situations where remembering past events can be beneficial, we've developed two universal networks capable of learning continuous-time autonomous systems that take the past into account. Additionally, we've shown that these networks can be extended to predict the behavior of systems whose governing equations are unknown or too complex to be solved analytically.

To deal with situations that don't fit perfectly into known models, we've developed an alternative approach that integrates a detailed model with learning techniques. This approach can be applied to complex systems whose behavior depends on various factors such as individual characteristics or environmental influences. However, this method requires significant computational resources due to the large data sets involved, so we've developed an efficient way to reduce the necessary data for such studies by identifying patterns in the data that other methods can't capture.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting finding. While most of these cores are significantly cooler, with an average temperature of around 18 Kelvin, a notable subgroup with temperatures around 28 Kelvin still exhibits a relatively large mass range, spanning almost three orders of magnitude. This discovery implies the existence of warmer cores that haven't yet transformed into colder, star-forming cores. Considering the cloud's distance of around 1.5 kiloparsecs and its relatively low density, it's likely that these warmer cores will eventually heat up in response to the influence of nearby massive star formation. This development could have significant consequences, as it may suppress the formation of additional massive stars within the cloud. A deeper understanding of core temperatures and their relationship to both physical properties and the formation of massive stars is ultimately essential for predicting the cloud's future stellar population. Observations of infrared emission could help gather this understanding, thanks to their sensitivity to cooler gas. Nonetheless, it's proposed that cores with sufficient mass and kinetic energy will ultimately develop into massive stars. If this prediction holds true, it's possible that only the largest cores, with masses exceeding 10 solar masses, will undergo significant temperature increases before initiating a massive star formation process. A proposed protocol for identifying massive core candidates within a given molecular cloud has also been developed, with potential applications for other clouds as well.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. To better study this possibility, researchers used a unique simulation tool called PopSyCLE to model different types of primordial black holes and their effects on nearby stars. They discovered that the tool's predictions align well with observations of microlensing events. Furthermore, the study found varying ranges of possible primordial black hole masses, from a specific range consistent with the 3.5 K cosmic microwave background anomaly to ranges that could potentially explain all of the universe's dark matter. Notably, the study found that, if primordial black holes explain dark matter, we can expect to see specific gravitational lensing events, which can be detected with current technology.

We've studied a system of hard wedges formed by three balls within the target space and obtained distinct phases with tetrahedral, 12 face cube, and frustum configurations. Our system naturally exhibits an order-disorder process similar to the structural transitions observed in certain colloidal systems and also shows triangular and face-centered cubic phases with internal distortions. This study sheds light on the underlying mechanisms driving the transitions between these phases and also demonstrates the presence of soft modes in certain arrangements, indicating their metastability.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial role of special tokens in handling sequences.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. Unlike a straightforward preference ranking where we compare two options at a time, this problem involves considering multiple items for addition. To address this, we both proposed a new method involving a symmetric preference ranking and tested existing approaches, including a noisy conditional choice revealed ranking and a noisy ordinary regression. Through a detailed analysis of our findings based on actual user feedback, we examined the strengths and weaknesses of each method, discovered interesting insights, and ultimately identified which approach yielded more accurate results.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental findings. These findings also suggest a robust enthalpy-internal energy relation across varying temperatures and concentrations. Based on these conclusions, we introduce new definitions of "dynamic configurational entropy" and "dynamic enthalpy," which respectively rely on the transient hole fraction and the average energy of molecules during sub-NS timescales. Our primary discovery indicates a direct proportion between these dynamic properties and the thermodynamic ones, which aligns with some but not all of the existing numerical simulations on binary mixtures. Additionally, we observed that the ratio of dynamic to thermodynamic property has slower sub-nanosecond dynamics that gets closer to equilibrium as temperature increases and/or concentration diverges, indicating that dynamic and thermodynamic properties become more relative as conditions change.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their handling of this concept.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that allows direct focusing on relevant target words that follow previous ones more accurately. We further explore the integration of our mechanism with state-of-the-art decoder models and demonstrate significant improvements in translation quality on standard benchmarks.

This passage uses a structured approach to calculate Kontsevich weights for various graphs associated with complex vector fields of order k on Rk. We apply this calculation to determine a weighted sum formula for the multidimensional Wiener integral, which generalizes Novikov's formula for the integral on a single dimension. Our approach combines techniques from quantum mechanics, symplectic integration, and field decomposition in multicomplex space. We also leverage the representation of multicomplex space as a tensor product of unit balls in complex n-dimensional space for our derivation.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out and it's noted that in contrast, entanglement entropy does not yield information about the potential function's coupling strength.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely monitored and continuous monitoring scenarios. Furthermore, it highlights the advantages of the CTMC method over Cai, Song and Kou's approach, which relies on the charactristic equation.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and galaxy clusters may all play a role. Researchers conducted a study that simulated galaxy clusters taking into account magnetic fields, solar wind, and potential dark matter particles with masses between 10-100 GeV. This simulation found the magnitude of the magnetic field, solar wind properties, and DM particle masses to be crucial factors that might explain the gamma-ray flux observed at Earth. Results from this study also predict that upcoming CTA will observe a signal from galaxy clusters, with a probability of over 95%. Additionally, future HESS and CTA observations could verify the presence of DM particles with masses ranging from 10-100 GeV and amplitude of electron-positron pairs of around 10-30 %.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of whether its training data is accessible. Moreover, this technique can produce new explanations that go beyond the categories initially learned during training. It also has a significant application in discovering biases within datasets without needing additional labels. To facilitate further research, the LaViSE repository, containing associated code and pre-trained models, is publicly available.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we have discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling, which goes beyond standard models, significantly affects the interaction between neighboring electrons. Within reasonable limits of this additional interaction and phonon energy, we have observed a strong increase in the copper oxide bond and a characteristic peak in the electron-dressed vertex, both of which are characteristic features observed in one-dimensional cuprate materials. Our results indicate that long-range electron-phonon coupling is a crucial factor in the interaction between neighboring electrons, supporting experimental observations. Furthermore, we have simulated the high-temperature superconducting gap in one-dimensional cuprate materials and found that long-range electron-phonon coupling and an exponential decay of the electron-phonon coupling with the distance between copper and oxygen sites are both necessary conditions for high-temperature superconductivity.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify crucial indicators and causal links related to the 90-90-90 targets. This method preserves critical information about key factors, in contrast to existing approaches which often result in significant data loss. When applied to the Malawi HIV assessment data set, our approach yielded notable results, identifying key indicators and providing valuable insights into the HIV transmission dynamics in the population.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state with topological defects generates topological solitons. The skyrmion lattice initially stable within a limited temperature and magnetic field range undergoes gradual destabilization as temperature or magnetic field increases, eventually transforming into a state rich in solitons. The amount of topological charge associated with each soliton remains constant despite variations in the lattice dislocation density. A sudden increase in the skyrmion lattice's topological charge as the system crosses a first-order phase transition triggers the formation of solitons. Theoretical model based on magnetization curves suggests a first-order phase transition due to differences in skyrmion and dislocation free energy at low magnetic field values. A potential energy reduction resulting from soliton formation is attributed to electron spin scattering decrease within the system, whereas the system's energy dissipation may increase due to dislocation movement. A consistent theoretical description of the system's behavior can be achieved only by considering the inherent magnetic disorder, thus resolving the discrepancy between experimental and theoretical topological charge values observed in previous research.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types and their underlying structure, 
rather than estimation methodologies, aiming to highlight innovative 
research avenues and applicable areas which are still underdeveloped.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models. By leveraging a hybrid approach that combines predictive and uncertainty assessments, we design novel reversible steganographic algorithms based on Bayesian Neural Networks. A distinct hybrid steeganographic approach is proposed, incorporating the integration of uncertainty and predictive capabilities. Experimental evaluations conducted on the ImageNet database demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method over the current best approach.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global convective dynamo simulations to investigate turbulent effects, which are measured by using the test-field method to calculate transport coefficients based on the mean-field framework. By incorporating all relevant turbulent effects, researchers are now able to accurately simulate geostrophic balance in the mean convective dynamo equilibrium, providing a more reliable understanding of the Sun's and stars' magnetic activity. The importance of including all turbulent effects was particularly apparent in the simulation of the Earth's core, where neglecting these effects results in unrealistic equilibrium solutions.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four plumes of molecular gas, possibly representing one-way outflows, connected to the galaxy's AGN activity. Three of these plumes, observed in the 12CO(1-2) and 13CO(1-2) spectral lines, are aligned with the galaxy's rotation axis, while an CO(1-2) spectral line observed in the 12CO(2-1) frequency is situated at 540 km/s. Two of the outflows, observed in the 12CO(1-2) and 13CO(1-2) spectral lines, are located at 260 km/s and are accompanied by a weakly emitted red lobe, indicating the start of a one-way outflow. The outflows' properties were calculated and it's hypothesized that they are driven by the galaxy's nuclear activity. The outflows' opening angles were calculated to be around 45 degrees. The gas within these outflows is about 220 km/s. The study's conclusions are that the galaxy NGC4945 possesses one-way outflows which are highly driven by the galaxy's nuclear activity. The study's conclusions are further supported by the study's findings that the galaxy's nuclear activity does not have co-propagating outflows, meaning that the study's findings conflict with the

The quasilinear model provides a conceptual framework for synchronizing kinetic and fluid descriptions in magnetized plasmas, enabling the incorporation of saturated turbulence phenomena into fluid models. For a specified distribution of electron energy, the model describes the evolution of the corresponding fluctuation pattern. A conservative variant of the Aristotle quasilinear model has been developed and proven to maintain long-term stability without leading to excessive growth of fluctuations. Additionally, the model's conservation properties have been accurately captured using a Galerkin formulation with a combination of Legendre polynomials, and the resulting numerical scheme maintains high-order accuracy and precision.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We also introduce an algorithm based on Kramers' method for variable stepsize SGLMs that incorporates non-uniform grid points. This new algorithm is then proven to be compatible with existing error estimates, and we demonstrate its efficiency using test problems from the DOOP package.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based platform for predicting the interactions between dimuonium (bound electron-muon pairs) and matter. MuMuPy allows users to input specific dimuonium and matter parameters and generates code that can be run manually or utilized through our accompanying web-based calculator. MuMuPy currently assesses three types of interactions: coupling constants, energy levels, and decay rates, which are calculated using numerical solutions to the Schrödinger equation, non-relativistic QED, and relativistic QED. MuMuPy's development aims to facilitate the interpretation of dimuonium spectroscopy, making it easier for users to input and output data. Furthermore, we outline potential applications for the proposed phi-meson production in the dimuonium decay channel.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem solution, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion explores key aspects observed in the IGM of our own Milky Way and neighboring galaxies, in addition to the challenges and opportunities presented by the study of dwarf galaxy interstellar material for the advancement of universal astrophysical knowledge.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle is resistant to collapse. The instability of the quasiparticle is heightened under the conditions: (i) an increase in the total number of bosonic excitations costing zero energy and (ii) an increase in the interaction strength between bosons and fermions. This model, which is applicable to doped Mott insulators, provides valuable insights into the collapse of quasiparticles in this context. Furthermore, it also sheds light on the quasiparticle collapse's rareness in systems featuring numerous quasiparticle-carrying processes.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence function. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. Alongside this, we initiate the corresponding analysis for the braided invertible groups $\widehat{BIF}$, $\widehat{BIP}$, and $\widehat{BIP}^*$.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been made publicly available on the HuggingFace Transformers library.

This study determines the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. Initially, we conduct an extensive survey to pinpoint relevant characteristics and demonstrate its effectiveness in filtering unqualified workers. Subsequently, we design two evaluation tasks aimed at evaluating annotation quality before undertaking a comprehensive study on how instructions and rewards impact annotation accuracy. Ultimately, we train and test reliable annotators using a novel loss function and make our annotated dataset available to the public.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen advancements with the pre-training of visual and text encoders. Yet, there's a discrepancy in capability between individual tokens of text and video due to their dissimilar lengths. Extending the cross-attention pattern from single-token association to token grouping enables longer-length data matching but introduces inefficiency and redundancy, necessitating an appropriate balance. In response, we introduce a new family of length-matching transformers, where token grouping and selection are seamlessly integrated with length adaptation in a single network. Unlike conventional methods, our proposed TS2-Net can work efficiently with videos of any length without pre-defined pooling layers. Furthermore, token grouping can be manipulated to facilitate multi-token feature extraction for text data, thereby enhancing cross-modal understanding and retrieval performance. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this novel transformer model, which achieves significant length-matching accuracy and demonstrates superior performance in text-video retrieval and text-based video search experiments.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can appear naturally in new physics scenarios, especially in composite Higgs theories. It's been shown that existing experiments provide little restriction on these interactions, but they can potentially be detected at the Large Hadron Collider by looking at rare top decays and other reactions. Due to its size, the top quark offers ideal conditions for studying these interactions that don't exist for other flavour-changing particles.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new class of hybrid networks has been introduced that balance complex preferential attachment with simpler uniform attachment mechanisms. Our research delves into the properties of these directed hybrid networks with two different uniform attachment methods, retaining the core properties of preferential attachment but allowing for the coexistence of different attachment preferences. By manipulating the hybrid ratio, which affects the preference distributions of target nodes, our models display both small-scale similarities and significant deviations from the classic Barabasi-Albert model in terms of degree distribution, clustering, and hub centrality. While the directed networks exhibit triadic closure, they display two distinct clustering behaviors and a more intricate hub distribution. These networks have the capacity to be tailored for various applications due to the adjustable hybrid ratio and degree distribution.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique that uses a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interference signals (from IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.11 b/g and IEEE 802.15.4) amidst a signal, among various other applications, with an ensuing error rate of 0%. This method is quick and requires minimal configuration, supplementing with a deep neural network among our contributions. It has been effectively tested using a commercial wireless device and is compatible with current standards including IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.11 b/g and IEEE 802.15.4.

In the context of cosmic string gravity with a spatial dislocation defect, we investigate the interactions of charged Klein-Gordon particles, focusing on energy and charge correlations. The dislocation disarranges spacetime, leading to a non-integrable metric tensor. Lefter and Gogokhia developed the dislocation model, building on Som and Raychaudhuri's work, with our research being the first extension in this area. The study involves finding Klein-Gordon particle positive energy solutions using the complete set of equations, and from these solutions, we derive the dispersion relation, extract the one-dimensional probability current, and assess vorticity and energy correlations. The results show that energy is linked to charge when vorticity is present, confirming a notable aspect of dislocation effects.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 2.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton's spin are crucial for understanding the nucleon's internal structure.  Experimental research into the distribution of valence quarks (DVCS) and the parton distribution functions (PDFs) associated with it are significant for developing new knowledge.
